16: The word “now” has the sense of qualification for study; it should be understood that the treatise on the instruction in <s>Yoga</s> is undertaken. <s>Yoga</s> is <s>samādhi</s> (enstasis), and this is a universal property of the mind (<s>citta</s>). The states of mind are: scattered, stupefied, distracted, one-pointed, and restrained. There, when the mind is distracted, <s>samādhi</s> being subordinate to distraction does not belong on the side of <s>Yoga</s>
17: But that which, when the mind is one-pointed, illumines a real object, also diminishes the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), loosens the bonds of <s>karma</s> (action), and makes for restraint—this is termed discriminative (<s>saṃprajñāta</s>) <s>Yoga</s>; and it is accompanied by deliberation (<s>vitarka</s>), accompanied by reflection (<s>vicāra</s>), accompanied by bliss (<s>ānanda</s>), and accompanied by the sense of I-ness (<s>asmitā</s>), as we shall explain below. But when all the modifications are restrained, then it is non-discriminative (<s>asaṃprajñāta</s>) <s>samādhi</s>
18: Desiring to state its definition, this sūtra was set forth —
19: <s>Yoga</s> is the cessation of the modifications of the mind
21: Because the term “all” is not employed, even discriminative <s>Yoga</s> is also so called. For the mind (<s>citta</s>), by reason of its nature of manifestation, activity, and stability, is of the three <s>guṇas</s> (constituents)
22: The sattva-aspect of the mind, being of the nature of manifestation, when commingled with rajas and tamas, becomes fond of dominion and objects; that very mind, when pierced by tamas, becomes associated with non-dharma, ignorance, non-dispassion, and non-lordliness; that very mind, when the veil of delusion is worn thin, shining forth on all sides, and penetrated by mere rajas, becomes associated with dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and lordliness
23: That very mind, when free from the slight stain of rajas, established in its own nature, consisting only of the cognition of the otherness of sattva and <s>puruṣa</s> (<s>sattva</s>-<s>puruṣa</s> otherness-cognition), becomes associated with the meditation called the cloud of dharma (<s>dharmamegha</s>); that supreme is what meditators call discriminative knowledge (<s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>). The power of consciousness (<s>citi-śakti</s>), unchanging, not passing over to another, having shown its object, is pure and infinite, and is of the nature of the sattva-<s>guṇa</s>; and the discriminative knowledge (<s>vivekakhyāti</s>) is the opposite of this. Therefore, the mind, dispassionate even towards that knowledge, restrains that very cognition. In that state it becomes associated with latent impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>); that is seedless <s>samādhi</s>. There, nothing is cognized; therefore it is non-discriminative (<s>asaṃprajñāta</s>). Thus that <s>Yoga</s> is twofold, as the cessation of the modifications of the mind
24: When the mind is in that condition, in the absence of objects, what is the nature of the <s>puruṣa</s>, whose essence is the illumination of the intellect? —
25: Then there is abiding in the seer’s own nature
27: Abiding in one’s own nature—then the power of consciousness is as in isolation (<s>kaivalya</s>); but when the mind has arisen again, although it still exists in that way, it is not thus
28: How then? Because it presents an object —
29: Elsewhere there is conformity with the modifications
31: In emergence, the modifications of the mind are those whose function the <s>puruṣa</s> does not differ from; and thus there is one sūtra only: “seeing is just recognition; recognition is just seeing.” The mind (<s>citta</s>), like a loadstone, is helpful merely by proximity, and, being the seen, becomes one’s own—of the <s>puruṣa</s>, the master; therefore, the beginningless relation of the <s>puruṣa</s> is the cause in the cognition of the mind’s modifications
32: Now those, on the other hand, are to be restrained, the mind having a multiplicity [of them] —
33: The modifications are of five kinds, afflicted and non-afflicted
35: Afflicted are those whose cause is the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), which, becoming a field, lead to the accumulation of the deposit of <s>karma</s> (<s>karmāśaya</s>); non-afflicted are those whose object is recognition (<s>khyāti</s>) and which are opposed to dominion of the <s>guṇas</s> (constituents). Even [modifications] fallen into an afflicted stream are [sometimes] non-afflicted; even in the fissures of the afflicted they become non-afflicted; in the fissures of the non-afflicted, they are afflicted. Thus, impressions (<s>saṃskāras</s>) of the same kind are produced precisely by the modifications; and through the impressions, the modifications [arise]. In this way, the wheel of modifications and impressions revolves incessantly. Such being the case, the mind, its function exhausted, remains as if of the nature of its own self, or goes to dissolution; thus the modifications, afflicted and non-afflicted, are fivefold
36: Right knowledge, error, conceptual construction, sleep, and memory
38: Perception, inference, and authoritative testimony are means of right knowledge
40: Perception is the modification of the mind, chiefly a determination of the particular of an object whose nature is both general and particular, having that as its object, due to the tinging of the mind by an external thing through the channel of the senses; the result is the undifferentiated, personal cognition that is a modification of the mind; that the <s>puruṣa</s> experiences [that cognition] we shall establish below
41: Inference is that modification whose object is the relation—continuant among those of the same kind as what is to be inferred, and excluded from those of a different kind—being chiefly a determination of the general pertaining to that; for example, as motion to another place implies that the moon and stars move, like <s>Caitra</s>, while the <s>Vindhya</s> does not move, implying non-motion; what is seen or inferred by a trustworthy person (<s>āpta</s>) is taught elsewhere by a word, for the transmission of his own cognition, and from the word there arises in the hearer the modification whose object is that thing—this is authoritative testimony (<s>āgama</s>). But if the speaker is not trustworthy regarding the matter, not having seen or inferred it, that <s>āgama</s> wavers; whereas when the original teacher has seen or inferred the matter, it would be unwavering
42: Error is false cognition, established in a form other than that [of the object]
44: Why is that not a means of right knowledge? Because it is sublated by right knowledge, since a means of right knowledge has real things as its object; there, the sublation of a non-means of right knowledge by a means of right knowledge is observed—just as the seeing of two moons is sublated by the seeing of a single moon whose object is real. This is five-limbed ignorance; the afflictions are ignorance, I-ness, attachment, aversion, and clinging to life. These very [afflictions], with their own names, are darkness, delusion, great delusion, gloom, and utter gloom; these will be spoken of in connection with the impurity of the mind
45: Conceptual construction is a modification devoid of a real object, following upon verbal cognition
47: It does not admit of being superimposed as a means of right knowledge, nor as error; although devoid of a real object, a conventional usage grounded in the potency of verbal cognition is seen—for instance, “consciousness is the very nature of the <s>puruṣa</s>.” When consciousness itself is the <s>puruṣa</s>, then what here is designated by what and by whom?
48: And a modification occurs in designation—just as “Caitra’s is the cow.” Likewise, [we say] “the <s>puruṣa</s>, whose property is that of the negated object, is inactive,” “the arrow stands,” “it will stand,” “it stood”—upon the cessation of motion, only the verbal root-meaning is apprehended; likewise, [when one says] “the <s>puruṣa</s> is of the property of non-arising,” only the absence of the property of arising is apprehended, not a property inhering in the <s>puruṣa</s>. Therefore that property is conceptualized, and yet there is usage
49: Sleep is the modification having as its support a cognition of absence
51: And this, upon waking, is a specific cognition discerned by reflective awareness; how so? “I slept happily; my mind is clear; it makes my discernment skillful; I slept unhappily; my mind is torpid; it wanders, unsettled; I slept in deep stupefaction; my limbs are heavy; my mind is weary; it stands as if sluggish and robbed,” yet indeed this reflective awareness would not occur for one who is awakened if there were no prior experience of a cognition, and the memories that rely on that, having that as their object, would not exist; therefore sleep is a specific cognition, and it too, like the other-cognitions, is to be restrained in <s>samādhi</s> (enstasis)
52: Memory is the non-loss of what has been experienced as an object
54: Is it the mind’s cognition that remembers, or is it the object? The cognition, tinged by the graspable, shining forth in the dual form of graspable and grasping, initiates an impression of its own kind; that impression, being its own revealer, produces a memory of precisely that form, having the dual nature of graspable and grasping
55: Therein, understanding is preceded by the form of grasping; memory is preceded by the form of the graspable; and it is twofold—both cultivated-to-be-remembered and uncultivated-to-be-remembered; in dream it is cultivated-to-be-remembered, whereas in the waking time it is uncultivated-to-be-remembered; all memories arise from the experience of right knowledge, error, conceptual construction, sleep, and memory; and all these modifications are of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion; and pleasure, pain, and delusion should be explained among the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions): attachment (<s>rāga</s>) accompanies pleasure, aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>) accompanies pain, and delusion is in fact ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>)
56: All these modifications are to be restrained; upon their restraint, <s>samādhi</s> is either discriminative (<s>saṃprajñāta</s>) or non-discriminative (<s>asaṃprajñāta</s>)
57: Now, as to the means for their restraint—
58: By practice and dispassion is their restraint
60: The river of mind, so called, flows both ways; it flows toward the auspicious and it flows toward the inauspicious; that which slopes toward the field of <s>viveka</s> (discriminative insight), weighted in advance toward <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation), that carries the auspicious; weighted in advance toward saṃsāra and sloping toward non-<s>viveka</s>, it carries the inauspicious; there, by dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>) the current toward objects is dammed up, and by practice of the vision of <s>viveka</s> the current of <s>viveka</s> is opened—thus the restraint of the mind’s modifications depends on both
61: There, effort toward steadiness is practice
63: The steadiness is the tranquil, even flow of a mind devoid of modifications; the effort for that—energy, vigor, zeal—for the desire to mature that, the undertaking of the means to accomplish it is practice
64: And this, practiced for a long time, without interruption, and with reverence, becomes well-founded
66: Practiced for a long time, practiced without interruption, practiced with reverence; brought to completion by austerity (<s>tapas</s>), celibate conduct (<s>brahmacarya</s>), knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>), and faith (<s>śraddhā</s>), endowed with reverence, it becomes well-founded; “quickly” means “not overpowered by the impression of emergence,” that is, not overmastered by the domain of distraction
67: Dispassion is the mastery-designated state of one who is without thirst for objects seen and heard-about
69: For one without thirst for visible objects—women, food and drink, lordly power—and for one without thirst for heard-about objects—attainment of heaven, disembodiment, and dissolution into <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature)—even in contact with divine and non-divine objects, for a mind that, through the power of discriminative contemplation (<s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>), sees the defects of objects, dispassion, called mastery, is of the nature of non-indulgence, devoid of what is to be shunned and what is to be taken up
70: That which is higher is indifference to the <s>guṇas</s> (constituents) through knowledge of the <s>puruṣa</s> (person)
72: He who sees the faults in objects seen and heard-about, being dispassionate, through the practice of the vision of the <s>puruṣa</s> (person), whose intellect, nourished by purity and discriminative discernment (<s>praviveka</s>), becomes dispassionate toward the <s>guṇas</s> (constituents), which possess the properties of manifest and unmanifest—this twofold is dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>). Of these, that which is higher is nothing but the lucidity of knowledge; when this arises, the yogin, with recognition newly arisen, thinks thus—“what was to be attained has been attained, the <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) that were to be eradicated are exhausted, the course of becoming, whose joints are interlinked, is cut; because of the non-break [of this state], one, having been born, dies, and dying is born”—dispassion is the very highest limit of knowledge; indeed, for this very one, isolation (<s>kaivalya</s>) is immediate
73: Now, by the two means, when the modifications of the mind have been restrained, how is it said that <s>samādhi</s> (enstasis) is discriminative (<s>saṃprajñāta</s>),—
74: By following upon the forms of vitarka (discursive examination), vicāra (subtle reflection), bliss (<s>ānanda</s>), and I-am-ness (<s>asmitā</s>) there is discriminative <s>samādhi</s>
76: Vitarka is the gross engagement of the mind with a support; subtle is vicāra; <s>ānanda</s> is delight; <s>asmitā</s> is a cognition that is of one essence [with its object]. Therein, the first <s>samādhi</s>, accompanied by the first four, is with vitarka; the second, lacking vitarka, is with vicāra; the third, lacking vicāra, is with bliss; the fourth, lacking that, is mere I-am-ness—thus all these <s>samādhis</s> are with a support
77: Now, as for non-discriminative <s>samādhi</s> (<s>asaṃprajñāta</s>): what is its means and what its nature?—
78: Another [<s>samādhi</s>] preceded by the practice whose idea is cessation, with only impressions remaining
80: When all modifications have subsided, the restraint of the mind, with only impressions remaining, is non-discriminative <s>samādhi</s>; for that the supreme dispassion is the means. For practice with a support is not suitable for accomplishing that; therefore the idea of cessation, being without a real object, is made the support; and that is devoid of content. Indeed, preceded by the practice of that, the mind becomes supportless, as if it had attained non-existence—this is seedless <s>samādhi</s>, non-discriminative
81: Now this indeed is twofold—having the [meditative] means as its basis, and having becoming as its basis. Of these, the one having means as its basis belongs to yogins—
82: The one having becoming as its basis belongs to the disembodied and to those dissolved into <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature)
84: For the disembodied gods it is the one based on becoming; for they, with a mind making use only of their own latent impressions, experiencing as it were the state of isolation (<s>kaivalya</s>), carry over into the ripening of their own impressions that which is of the same kind; likewise, those dissolved into <s>Prakṛti</s>, while the mind, along with its sphere of operation, is merged into <s>Prakṛti</s>, experience as it were the state of isolation, until the mind returns again by force of the residual claim to activity
85: For others, it is preceded by faith (<s>śraddhā</s>), vigor (<s>vīrya</s>), memory (<s>smṛti</s>), <s>samādhi</s>, and insight (<s>prajñā</s>)
87: The one based on means belongs to yogins. Faith is the serenity of the mind; for she, auspicious like a mother, protects the yogin. For him who has faith and desires <s>viveka</s> (discriminative insight), vigor arises; when vigor has arisen, memory is established; when memory is established, the mind, undisturbed, becomes enstatically collected; for the one whose mind is collected, insight-as-discrimination (<s>prajñā-viveka</s>) returns, by which he knows a thing as it really is; from the practice of that and from dispassion toward each respective object, there is non-discriminative <s>samādhi</s>
88: Now these yogins are nine, having mild, middling, and excessive measures of the means. Namely—mild means, middling means, and excessively strong means. Therein the mild means is threefold—mildly impelled, moderately impelled, intensely impelled; so too the middling means, and so too the excessively strong means. Among those of excessively strong means—
89: For those intensely impelled it is near at hand
91: Both the attainment of <s>samādhi</s> and the fruit of <s>samādhi</s> occur
92: From mildness, middlingness, and excessiveness, there is yet further distinction
94: Mild-intense, middling-intense, and supremely-intense—that is the classification. Even beyond that there is a distinction. From that very distinction too: for one with mild-intense impulsion it is near at hand; from that, for one with middling-intense impulsion it is nearer; than that, for one with supremely-intense impulsion, even with a supremely-great means, the attainment of <s>samādhi</s> (enstasis) and the fruit of <s>samādhi</s> are nearest
95: Is it only from this that <s>samādhi</s> becomes nearest? Or, upon its attainment, is there perhaps some other means as well, or not—
98: By devotion, by a distinctive form of bhakti, <s>Īśvara</s>, being drawn toward him, favors him by mere contemplation; and even from that mere contemplation, for the yogin the attainment of <s>samādhi</s>, nearest of all, and the fruit of <s>samādhi</s> arise
99: Now, is this <s>Īśvara</s>, distinct from <s>Pradhāna</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>, who or what is he, or not—
100: <s>Īśvara</s> is a special <s>puruṣa</s> untouched by the afflictions, actions, fruition, and deposits of latent impressions
102: The afflictions (<s>kleśas</s>) are ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) and the rest. The actions are meritorious and demeritorious. Their fruit is fruition (<s>vipāka</s>). The dispositions (<s>vāsanā</s>), corresponding to those, are the deposits (<s>āśayas</s>). And these, while occurring in the mind, are imputed to the <s>puruṣa</s>, for he is the enjoyer of that fruit; just as victory or defeat, though occurring among the fighters, is imputed to the lord. He who is not touched by this enjoyment is the special <s>puruṣa</s>, <s>Īśvara</s>
103: But then, since isolation (<s>kaivalya</s>) has been attained, there are indeed many isolated ones; they, having cut the three bonds, have attained <s>kaivalya</s>, and with <s>Īśvara</s> there is neither past nor future connection of that sort. Just as for one liberated the prior series of bondage is cognized, not so for <s>Īśvara</s>; or just as for one merged into <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature) a subsequent series of bondage is conceivable, not so for <s>Īśvara</s>. But he is ever liberated, ever the Lord
104: Now, the perpetual excellence of <s>Īśvara</s>, arising from the adoption of exceedingly pure <s>sattva</s> (lucidity), is that with a cause or without a cause? Its cause is scripture (<s>śāstra</s>)
105: And what is the cause of scripture? The cause is exceedingly pure <s>sattva</s>
106: Between these two—excellence of scripture and the presence of <s>Īśvara</s>—there is a beginningless relation. From this it follows: he is ever the Lord, ever liberated. And that lordship of his is free from superiority and from parity; by no other lordship is that surpassed, for whatever would surpass it would itself be that very thing. Therefore, he in whom there is the extremity of attainment of lordship is <s>Īśvara</s>. Nor is there lordship equal to that. Why? For two equals, if, with respect to one and the same object simultaneously desired, one were to have “let this be new, let that be old,” then, upon the success of the one, because of the obstruction of the other’s prerogative, inferiority would result. And for two equals there is no simultaneous attainment of an object simultaneously desired, because the object is mutually opposed. Therefore, he whose lordship is free from parity and superiority—he alone is <s>Īśvara</s>; and he is a special <s>puruṣa</s>
108: There, the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed
110: This grasping—beyond the senses—of each and every collection of past, future, and present, whether little or much, this is the seed of omniscience; where this, growing, is unsurpassed, he is omniscient. There is an extremity of attainment of the seed of omniscience, since, having superiority, it is measurable; where there is the extremity of attainment of knowledge, he is omniscient; and he is a special <s>puruṣa</s>
111: And moreover, where there is only a general summative conclusion, inference, having accomplished the removal of [ignorance] to that extent, is not capable with respect to the ascertainment of the particular; therefore, the ascertainment of his particular designations and the like is to be traced from scripture (<s>āgama</s>), even though there is no benefaction to himself, the benefaction to beings is the purpose, “By instructing in the dharma of knowledge I shall lift up the transmigrating <s>puruṣas</s> at the [periodic] dissolution of a cycle and at the great dissolution,” and thus it has been said—“the knower of the beginning (<s>ādi-vidvān</s>), having assumed a mind created by will (<s>nirmāṇa-citta</s>), out of compassion, the Blessed Supreme Seer (<s>bhagavān paramarṣi</s>) spoke a scripture (<s>tantra</s>) to <s>Āsuri</s>, who was desiring to know,”
113: He is also the teacher of the former ones, because he is not delimited by time
115: For the former teachers indeed are limited by time; he, with respect to whom time does not recur as a delimiter, this very one is the teacher even of the former ones; as at the beginning of this creation he is to be understood as perfected through the excellence of his course, so also in creations that have passed beyond, and so forth
116: His denotative word is the <s>praṇava</s> (the syllable Om)
118: The denoted is <s>Īśvara</s> of the <s>praṇava</s>; now, is the relation of denoted and denotative for this established by convention, or is it as established as the illumination of a lamp?
119: The relation of the denoted, which is established, with the denotative, is established; and convention, for <s>Īśvara</s>, indicates precisely the already-established meaning; as the relation of father and son, being as it is, is indicated by convention—“this is his father, this is his son”; so too, even in other creations, the convention is made with regard to the powers of denoted and denotative; those who rely on scripture assert that the relation of word and meaning is eternal by reason of the constant mutual apprehension
120: For the yogin who has understood the denoted-and-denotative relationship—
121: Its recitation and the contemplation of its meaning
123: The recitation of the <s>praṇava</s>, and the contemplation of <s>Īśvara</s> who is signified by the <s>praṇava</s>; then, for this yogin who recites the <s>praṇava</s> and contemplates the meaning of the <s>praṇava</s>, the mind becomes one-pointed; and so it has been said—
125: From self-recitation (<s>svādhyāya</s>) one should enter into <s>yoga</s>, and from <s>yoga</s> one should undertake self-recitation; by the accomplishment of self-recitation and <s>yoga</s>, the Supreme Self (<s>paramātman</s>) becomes manifest
127: And further, what accrues to him—
128: Thence, the attainment of inward consciousness and also the absence of obstacles
130: Those obstacles beginning with illness do not occur at all because of devotion to <s>Īśvara</s>; likewise, there is for him the vision of his own nature; just as <s>Īśvara</s>, the <s>puruṣa</s>, is pure, serene, alone, untouched by affliction, so this one too attains that <s>puruṣa</s> who, being self-cognizant over against the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>), is his own self
131: Now then, which are the obstacles—those perturbations of the mind? And what are they, and how many—
132: Illness, stagnation, doubt, carelessness, laziness, non-abstinence, false seeing, non-attainment of a level, and instability—these are the distractions of the mind; those are the obstacles
134: The distractions of the mind are nine obstacles; these occur together with mental modifications, and in the absence of these, the previously mentioned mental modifications do not occur; illness is the inequality of the elements that compose the body; stagnation is the mind’s incapacity for action; doubt is a cognition that grasps both alternatives—“thus it is,” “thus it is not”; carelessness is the non-cultivation of the means to <s>samādhi</s>; laziness is the non-activity of body and mind due to heaviness; non-abstinence is greed, consisting in the mind’s conjunction with objects; false seeing is cognition as error (<s>viparyaya-jñāna</s>); non-attainment of a level is the non-attainment of the level of <s>samādhi</s>; instability is the non-establishment of the mind upon a level that has been attained—for, when the attainment of <s>samādhi</s> has indeed been secured, it should be established in that state; these nine—distractions of the mind—are called the impurities of <s>yoga</s>, the adversaries of <s>yoga</s>, the obstacles to <s>yoga</s>
135: Suffering, dejection, trembling of the limbs, and inhalation-exhalation are concomitants of distraction
137: Suffering is threefold: pertaining to oneself (<s>ādhyātmika</s>), pertaining to beings/external elements (<s>ādhibhautika</s>), and pertaining to the divine (<s>ādhidaivika</s>). That by which living beings are struck, for the removal of which they strive—that is suffering. Dejection (<s>daurmanasya</s>) is an agitation of the mind due to the frustration of desire. That which makes the limbs tremble and shake—that is trembling of the limbs (<s>aṅgamejayatva</s>). When <s>Prāṇa</s> sips in the external air, that is inhalation (<s>śvāsa</s>); when it expels the air from the mouth, that is exhalation (<s>praśvāsa</s>). These are concomitants of distraction; these occur for one whose mind is distracted. For one whose mind is enstatically collected, these do not occur
138: Now, these distractions are opposed to <s>samādhi</s>; they are to be suppressed by these two—by practice (<s>abhyāsa</s>) and dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>). Thereupon, bringing to a conclusion the scope of practice, he says this—
139: For the prevention of that, the practice of one-tattva (one principle) [is to be undertaken],
141: For the prevention of distraction, one should practice fixing the mind upon a single principle (<s>ekatattva-avalambana</s>). But for one whose mind is only a momentary cognition, fixed upon a specifically opposed object and restricted to it, for him the entire mind is not one-pointed at all but distracted. If, on the contrary, withdrawing this [mind] from everything, it is collected upon a single object, then it becomes one-pointed, and therefore it is not to be restricted to an opposed object
142: And if someone thinks the mind is one-pointed by a stream of similar cognitions—if his one-pointedness is a property of a stream-mind, then there is no one [mind], for a stream-mind is momentary; or if it is a property of only a portion of the stream, then whether the stream of similar cognitions or of dissimilar cognitions, being restricted to an opposed object, it would be one-pointed—thus the consequence that a distracted mind would be untenable. Therefore, the mind is one, established with respect to many objects
143: And if cognitions, not connected with one and the same mind, differing in their own natures, were to arise, then how would one who has seen one cognition remember another cognition? And for the heap of karmic deposits (<s>karmāśaya</s>) accrued by one cognition, some other cognition would be the enjoyer. Even if in some way this were being collected in <s>samādhi</s>, behold the fallacy of the maxim of cow-dung and milk (gomaya–pāyasī)—[an incongruous mixture]
144: What is more, the otherness of mind would result in a denial of one’s own experience. How so? The cognition “I touch what I have seen, and I see what I have not touched,” the ‘I’-cognition, though every cognition is distinct, is presented as non-distinct in the cognizer. This cognition ‘I’, whose nature is non-difference within the scope of a single cognition—how, existing in minds absolutely distinct, would it rely upon one single common cognizer? And this non-different ‘I’-cognition, grasped in one’s own experience, is not overruled in its supremacy by another means of knowledge; and another means of knowledge gains its very operation by the power of perception. Therefore, the mind is one and is established with respect to many objects
145: For the one whose mind is thus established, what purification is indicated in scripture? How so—
146: By the cultivation of friendliness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward those who are the subjects of happiness, suffering, merit, and demerit, there is clarity of mind
148: Therein, toward all beings who have come into the enjoyment of happiness, one should cultivate friendliness (<s>maitrī</s>); toward those who are suffering, compassion (<s>karuṇā</s>); toward those possessed of merit, sympathetic joy (<s>muditā</s>); toward those of unmeritorious conduct, equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>). Thus, for one who cultivates in this way, a white (pure) <s>dharma</s> arises; thereafter the mind becomes serene, and being serene, one-pointed, it attains the abiding state
149: Or, by exhalation and retention of the <s>Prāṇa</s>,
151: The vomiting forth (expulsion) of the air of the mouth, through the nostrils by a special exertion—this is exhalation (<s>pracchardana</s>); retention (<s>vidhāraṇa</s>) is <s>prāṇāyāma</s> (breath-regulation); by these two one should bring about the steadiness of the mind
152: Or the arising activation furnished with an object becomes a fetter (support) for the steadiness of the mind,
154: For one who holds (fixes) at the tip of the nose, the consciousness-of-scent that is divine—this is the activation of scent; at the tip of the tongue, consciousness-of-taste; on the palate, consciousness-of-form; in the middle of the tongue, consciousness-of-touch; at the root of the tongue, consciousness-of-sound—these activations, having arisen, bind the mind to steadiness, dispel doubt, and become doorways to <s>samādhi-prajñā</s> (enstatic insight). From this it is to be understood that, when an activation arises with respect to moons, suns, planets, jewels, lamp-rays, and so on, it is indeed endowed with an object; for although the true nature of a given object, grasped by scripture (<s>śāstra</s>), inference, and the instruction of the teacher, is indeed existent as real by reason of their capacity to present the object as it is, nevertheless, so long as even a single portion of that [object] is not apprehended by one’s own organ, the whole remains, as it were, indirect, and with respect to subtle objects such as liberation (<s>apavarga</s>) and the like, it does not produce firm understanding. Therefore, solely for the fortifying of scripture, inference, and the teacher’s instruction, some particular object must necessarily be made directly perceptible. Then, when even a single portion of the object taught has been made perceptible, everything—even what has a subtle object, beginning from liberation—is trusted. It is for this very purpose that this mind-preparation is prescribed: when, among the non-fixed activations, mastery over their respective objects has arisen, one becomes competent to render this or that object directly perceptible. And when that is so, his faith (<s>śraddhā</s>), energy (<s>vīrya</s>), memory (<s>smṛti</s>), and enstasy (<s>samādhi</s>) will come to be without hindrance
155: Or, free from sorrow (<s>viśokā</s>), and luminous (<s>jyotiṣmatī</s>),
157: The earlier statement continues: an activation that has arisen is a fetter (support) for the establishment of the mind. For one who holds (fixes) in the lotus of the heart there is consciousness of intellect (<s>buddhi</s>); for the <s>buddhi-sattva</s> (the lucidity of the intellect) is radiant, like space; there, by excellence in steadiness, the activation is diversified in the form of the effulgence of sun, moon, planets, and jewels. Likewise, when the mind has entered into <s>asmitā</s> (I-am-ness), it becomes calm, infinite, consisting of mere <s>asmitā</s>, like a great ocean without waves. Regarding this it is said—
158: “Having followed the self as minute as an atom, ‘I am this’—thus far, he is conscious,”
159: Thus. These two—free from sorrow and endowed with an object—and the activation that is mere <s>asmitā</s>, are called luminous (<s>jyotiṣmatī</s>). By these the yogin’s mind attains the abiding state
160: Or the mind whose object is one who is free from passion (<s>vītarāga</s>),
162: Or the yogin’s mind, tinged by reliance upon the mind of one who is free from passion, attains the abiding state
163: Or reliance upon the cognition of dream or of sleep,
165: Either reliance upon dream-cognition or reliance upon sleep-cognition—of that form, the yogin’s mind attains the abiding state
166: Or by meditation on whatever is esteemed,
168: Whatever indeed is esteemed, let him meditate upon just that; there, having obtained steadiness, he attains an abiding state elsewhere as well
169: His mastery extends up to the limit of the minute atom and of the greatest magnitude,
171: For one settling into the subtle, the abiding state extends up to the limit of the minute atom; for one settling into the gross, the abiding state of the mind extends up to the limit of the greatest magnitude. Thus, as he pursues both extremes, the absence of obstruction for him—this is supreme mastery. Through that mastery, the yogin’s mind becomes complete, and no longer requires preparation brought about by practice
172: Now, for a mind that has obtained steadiness, what is the nature of samāpatti (enstatic attainment), and what is its object? This is explained—
173: For one whose activations are diminished, the samāpatti is the taking-on of the coloration of that [object] in the apprehender, the apprehension, and the apprehended, as of a flawless gem, standing upon that [object] and tinged by that
175: “Of diminished activations” means “of one whose conceptions have subsided.” “Like a flawless gem”—this is the adducing of an illustration; just as a crystal, due to the difference of its support, appears tinged with the forms corresponding to that support and shines forth in the shape of the support, so the mind, tinged by the support which is the apprehended object, having attained samāpatti on the apprehended, shines forth in the mode of the very form of the apprehended; tinged by subtle elements (<s>bhūta-sūkṣma</s>), having attained samāpatti on the subtle elements, it becomes an appearance of the very nature of the subtle elements; likewise, tinged by a gross support, having attained samāpatti on a gross form, it becomes an appearance of the gross form; likewise, tinged by the differentiations of the universe, having attained samāpatti on the differentiations of the universe, it becomes an appearance of the universal form
176: So too it should be understood in respect of the instruments of apprehension, namely the senses; tinged by the support which is apprehension, having attained samāpatti on apprehension, it shines forth in the mode of the very nature of apprehension; likewise, tinged by the support which is the apprehender-<s>puruṣa</s>, having attained samāpatti on the apprehender-<s>puruṣa</s>, it shines forth in the mode of the very nature of the apprehender-<s>puruṣa</s>; likewise, tinged by the support which is the liberated <s>puruṣa</s>, having attained samāpatti on the liberated <s>puruṣa</s>, it shines forth in the mode of the very nature of the liberated <s>puruṣa</s>. Thus, for a mind likened to a flawless gem, in respect of apprehender, apprehension, and apprehended—being <s>puruṣa</s>, senses, and elements—its being colored by whatever each of those is, and the assumption of the form of that in which it is established, that is what is called samāpatti
177: Therein, the samāpatti accompanied by conceptual differentiations of word, meaning, and cognition is savitarkā
179: For example, one perceives, without distinction, even of things that are distinct, “the word ‘cow’,” “the meaning ‘cow’,” “the cognition ‘cow’”; and when distinguished, there are other properties belonging to word, others belonging to meaning, others belonging to cognition—these have distinct pathways. There, if for the yogin who has entered samāpatti, the object such as “cow,” mounted in enstatic insight (<s>samādhi-prajñā</s>), nevertheless returns accompanied by conceptual differentiations of word, meaning, and cognition, that mixed samāpatti is called savitarkā
180: But when, upon the purification of the memory of the conventional association of word, in enstatic insight devoid of the conceptual constructions of hearing and inference, the object stands by its own nature alone, it is delimited solely as the mode of its own form; and that is nirvitarkā samāpatti—this is the supreme perception, and it is the seed of hearing and inference; thereafter hearing and inference arise from it; nor is that seeing conjoined with the knowledge of hearing and inference; therefore, the yogin’s seeing born of nirvitarka-samādhi is unmixed and not via another means of knowledge. By this sūtra the definition of nirvitarkā samāpatti is indicated—
181: When memory is purified, with the own-form appearing as if absent, there is a shining-forth of the mere object alone—this is nirvitarkā
183: That insight which, upon the purification of the memory of conceptual constructions arising from word-convention, hearing, and inference, having abandoned its own form as if it were its own insight-nature consisting in grasping, and being of the mere nature of the object alone, appears as if it had become the very form of the apprehended—that then is nirvitarkā samāpatti
184: And thus it has been explained: its initiation is by a single cognition; indeed, the world beginning with “cow” or with “pot” is of the nature of a particular accumulation of <s>artha</s>-atoms (object-atoms)
185: And that particular configuration, a common property of the subtle elements, being inferred by an effect that is manifest, appears along with its own revealing adjuncts; and when another property, like “pot-shard” and the like, arises, it disappears; this property is called the whole (avayavin). It is by that whole, which is one, great, minute, possessing contact, action-qualified, and impermanent, that dealings are carried on
186: But if, on the other hand, that particular accumulation is without a substrate (object), and the subtle cause is unapprehended for the non-conceptual, then, due to the absence of the whole (avayavin), the cognition not established in that very form is false cognition; thus, for the most part, everything would end up being false cognition. And then, would there even be right cognition, given the absence of an object? Whatever is apprehended is designated as a whole (avayavin). Therefore, there exists a whole which incurs ordinary dealings such as largeness, and it becomes the object of nirvitarkā samāpatti
187: By this very account, the savicārā and the nirvicārā, having subtle objects, have been explained
189: There, the samāpatti which is upon subtle elements (<s>bhūta-sūkṣma</s>) whose properties are manifest, yet bounded by the experience of place, time, and occasion, is called savicāra; and there too, that subtle element, endowed with manifest properties and graspable by a single intellect alone, becomes the support (ālambana) in enstatic insight (<s>samādhi-prajñā</s>)
190: But the samāpatti which, in every way and from every side, is upon those whose properties of quiescence and arising are inexpressible, not delimited, which accompany all properties, which are of the nature of all properties—that is called nirvicāra; for just such is that subtle element, and by this very its own form, having become the support, it tinges (imbues) the very nature of enstatic insight
191: And when the insight, being as if devoid of its own form, becomes mere object, then it is called nirvicāra. There, with a great object as its field, there are savitarkā and nirvitarkā; with a subtle object as its field, there are savicārā and nirvicārā; thus, for both, by this very nirvitarkā, the removal of conceptual construction (vikalpa) has been explained
192: And the condition of having a subtle object culminates in the unmarked (<s>aliṅga</s>)
194: For the earthy atom, the subtle object is the tanmātra of scent; for the aqueous, the tanmātra of taste; for the fiery, the tanmātra of form; for the airy, the tanmātra of touch; for the ākāśic, the tanmātra of sound. Their <s>ahaṃkāra</s> (I-maker); and for this too, the mere-mark (<s>liṅga-mātra</s>) is the subtle object; and for the mere-mark, the unmarked (<s>aliṅga</s>) is the subtle object. And beyond the unmarked there is no subtler. But is there not the <s>puruṣa</s> as subtle? True; yet, whereas beyond the marked the subtlety of the unmarked is affirmed, it is not so for the <s>puruṣa</s>; rather, the <s>puruṣa</s> does not become the concomitant cause (anvayi-kāraṇa) of the marked, though he is indeed a reason (hetu) [for its operation as an end]; therefore, unsurpassed subtlety is explained to be in <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter)
195: Those themselves are the seeded samādhi
197: Those four samāpattis have external objects as seeds; therefore samādhi too is with seed. Therein, with a gross object, there are savitarka and nirvitarka; with a subtle object, there are savicāra and nirvicāra—thus samādhi is enumerated in four ways
198: With skill (mastery) in nirvicāra, there is clarity of the inner self (<s>adhyātma-prasāda</s>)
200: The lucidity (vaiśāradyam) is the clear, steady flow of the luminous nature of the <s>buddhi-sattva</s>, from which impurity, veil, and stain have been removed, not overpowered by rajas and tamas; when this mastery in nirvicāra-samādhi arises, then for the yogin there is clarity of the inner self—namely, a bright light of insight, concerning real things, explicit, and in conformity with the sequence
201: Ascending to the serenity of insight, the wise one, not to be sorrowed over, beholds the sorrowing people,
202: like one standing upon a mountain beholds those on the ground
206: In that one whose mind is enstatically collected, the insight that arises has the designation ‘truth-bearing’; and it is apt to its name, for it bears only truth, and there is not even a scent of erroneous cognition therein
208: By scripture, by inference, and by the sap of meditative practice,
209: fashioning insight in three ways, one attains the highest <s>yoga</s>
212: Is of a different object than the insights from hearing and inference, because it has a specific object
214: Hearing is scripture-based cognition; that has a general object. For a specification cannot be expressed by scripture—why? because a word is not fixed by a convention made with respect to a specification. Likewise, inference too has only a general object; it is said, “Where there is presence, there is going; where there is absence, there is no going.” And by inference there is a general conclusion. Therefore, no specification at all is the object of hearing and inference,
215: Nor is there apprehension of this exceedingly subtle, obstructed, and remote entity by ordinary perception. Nor does the absence of this specification, which lacks a means of valid cognition, obtain; thus, it is only graspable by enstatic insight (<s>samādhi-prajñā</s>)—that specification occurs either pertaining to subtle elements (<s>bhūta-sūkṣma</s>) or pertaining to <s>puruṣa</s>. Therefore, that insight has a different object than hearing-based and inference-based insights, because it has a specific object,
216: Upon the obtaining of enstatic insight (<s>samādhi-prajñā</s>), for the yogin, a disposition fashioned by insight is born ever anew—
217: The disposition born from that restrains other dispositions
219: The disposition that arises from enstatic insight (<s>samādhi-prajñā</s>) suppresses the bed of dispositions produced by emergence. Because of overpowering the emergence-dispositions, the ideations originating from them do not occur; when ideations are restrained, samādhi is established; then there is insight born of samādhi, then dispositions fashioned by insight—thus an ever-new bed of dispositions is produced. Then again insight, then again dispositions, and so on; how then will that excess of dispositions not render the mind endowed with eligibility for action? Those dispositions fashioned by insight do not render the mind possessed of eligibility for action, because they are causes of the destruction of the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>); indeed, they bring the mind down from its own activity. For the activity of the mind culminates in discriminative knowledge (<s>khyāti</s>)—so it is,
221: Upon the restraint of even that, owing to the restraint of all, there is seedless samādhi
223: That does not merely oppose enstatic insight (<s>samādhi-prajñā</s>); it also restrains even the dispositions fashioned by insight. Why? Because the disposition born of restraint suppresses the dispositions born of samādhi,
224: From the experience of the temporal sequence of the abiding of restraint, the existence of dispositions produced by the mind-in-restraint is to be inferred. Together with the dispositions produced by emergence, restraint, and samādhi, as well as those that partake of isolation (<s>kaivalya</s>), the mind dissolves into its own nature when it is established therein; therefore, those dispositions, being opposed to the mind’s eligibility-for-action, do not become causes of its continuance. Since the mind, having completed its function, together with the dispositions that partake of isolation, turns back, when that has turned back, the <s>puruṣa</s>, established only in his own form, is therefore called pure, alone, liberated,
225: Thus, in the venerable Yoga treatise, the Sāṃkhya exposition of <s>Śrī</s><s>Patañjali</s>, in the venerable <s>Vyāsa</s>’s Bhāṣya, the first book, the Samādhi-pāda, [is concluded],
227: The yoga for one whose mind is collected has been taught. How should one whose mind is outwardly active nevertheless be yoked to yoga?—this is begun—
228: Austerity (<s>tapas</s>), self-recitation (<s>svādhyāya</s>), and dedication to <s>Īśvara</s> (<s>Īśvara-praṇidhāna</s>) are the <s>kriyā-yoga</s>
230: Without austerity (<s>tapas</s>), yoga does not succeed; for the impurity—variegated by beginningless karma, afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>), and impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>), and by the nets of objects that present themselves—does not come to be broken up without austerity—therefore the adoption of austerity. And that, being a pacifier of the mind, unobstructive, is to be practiced by him—so he holds,
231: Self-recitation (<s>svādhyāya</s>) is the japa of purifiers such as the syllable Om (<s>praṇava</s>), or the study of the scriptures of liberation; dedication to <s>Īśvara</s> (<s>Īśvara-praṇidhāna</s>) is the offering of all actions to the supreme Teacher and the renunciation of their fruits,
233: Is for cultivating samādhi and for attenuating the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>)
235: For, when cultivated, that [kriyā-yoga] fosters samādhi and attenuates the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>). The afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) having been made thin become, as it were, seeds scorched by the fire of discriminative cognition (<s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>), of the nature of non-germination, so that they will not produce [future fruition]. Because of the attenuation of those, a mere discriminative knowledge of the difference between <s>Sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s> (<s>sattva-puruṣa-anyatā-mātra-khyāti</s>), a subtle insight whose mandate (scope) has been completed, is contrived for reversal (return-flow, <s>pratiprasava</s>)
236: Now then, which are the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) and how many are they—
237: Ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>), I-notion (<s>asmitā</s>), attachment (<s>rāga</s>), aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>), and clinging-to-life (<s>abhiniveśa</s>) are the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>)
239: Afflictions—there are five; that is to say, they are misapprehensions (viparyaya). As they vibrate, they consolidate the jurisdiction of the <s>guṇa</s>-s, establish transformation, raise up the current of cause and effect, and, having become a system of mutual favoring of one another, they also bring about karma and its ripening
240: Ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) is the field for the others—whether dormant, thinned, interrupted, or fully manifest
242: Here, ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) is the field, the generative ground, for the subsequent ones beginning with <s>asmitā</s>, in their fourfold modes of dormancy, thinness, interruption, and manifestness. There, what is dormancy? The coming to have seed-nature, consisting in mere potency established in the mind. Its awakening, upon the presence of a support (object), is the coming into the forefront. For one who possesses discriminative cognition (<s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>), even when the support has come to the forefront for the one whose affliction-seeds are burnt, that [affliction] is no longer there—how could there be a sprouting of a burnt seed? Therefore, he whose afflictions are exhausted is a skillful person in his final body, so it is said. Right there, that state of burnt-seed-ness is the fifth stage of the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>), not elsewhere. When the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) yet exist, then their seed-capability is burnt—hence, even when the object is present to view, there is no awakening of these; thus dormancy is explained as the non-sprouting of burnt seeds
243: Thinness is stated thus: afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) struck down by cultivating the opposite (pratipakṣa-bhāvanā) become thin. Likewise, being cut off again and again, they arise repeatedly each in their own fashion—hence they are ‘interrupted.’ How so? Because, at the time of attachment (<s>rāga</s>), hatred (<s>krodha</s>) is not seen; for, at the time of attachment, hatred does not arise. And attachment, though seen in some case, is not present with respect to another object. It is not that because <s>Caitra</s> is infatuated with one woman he is dispassionate toward other women; rather, there the attachment has obtained operative status, whereas elsewhere it will have to-be-operative status. Thus at that time it becomes dormant, thin, and interrupted
244: That which has obtained operative status with respect to its object is ‘manifest.’ All of these, indeed, do not transgress being afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) with respect to an object. Which, then, is an affliction—interrupted, dormant, thinned, or manifest? It is said: this is indeed true; but these modes of interruption and so on belong only to the particular ones [present]. Just as that which has ceased through the cultivation of the opposite becomes manifest again by its own revealers, so it is. All these afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) are divisions of ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>). Why? Because ignorance floods into all. Whatever is made to appear as the real by ignorance—that alone the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) adhere to; they are encountered at the time of a cognitional inversion (viparyāsa-pratyaya), and, as ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) is being attenuated, they too are attenuated along with it
245: There, the nature of ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) is stated—
246: Ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) is the ascription of permanence, purity, happiness, and selfhood to what is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self
248: Permanence is ascribed to the impermanent—i.e., to an effect; for example: “The earth is constant,” “The heaven with moon and stars is constant,” “The dwellers in heaven are immortal,” likewise, purity is ascribed to the body, which is supremely loathsome—
250: Because of its position, its seed, its supports, its discharges, and its very perishing,
251: the body, being only something to be placed down, is known by the learned to be impure,”
253: Thus, the apprehension of purity is seen in what is impure. “She—charming like a fresh crescent of the moon, as though fashioned from honey and nectar, as if having burst through the moon and come forth—is perceived; with eyes long like the petals of a blue lotus, with the two gaze-organs pregnant with coquettish play, as if she were comforting the world of living beings”—what relation does there exist of whom with whom? And so it is that, in the impure, there is a cognition inverted as purity. By this, a cognition of merit (virtue) is likewise explained in what is demerit (vice), and a cognition of value (meaning) in what is non-value (non-meaning),
254: Likewise, regarding pain, he will state the cognition as happiness—
255: “Because of the pains of transformation, ardor (burning), and saṃskāra, and because of the mutual opposition of the functions of the <s>guṇa</s>-s, all is pain indeed for the discerning,”
256: Thus there, the cognition as happiness is ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>). Likewise, the cognition as self in what is non-self—whether in external implements, conscious or non-conscious; or in the body as the seat of enjoyment; or in the mind as an instrument of <s>puruṣa</s>—the cognition as self in the non-self, indeed. Likewise, this has been said here—
257: “Manifest or unmanifest, <s>Sattva</s>, being apprehended as the self, he delights in its success, thinking it the success of the self; he sorrows at its misfortune, thinking it the misfortune of the self; he is entirely unawakened,”
258: And this ignorance has four feet (aspects), and is the root of this continuum of afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) and of the karmic deposit (<s>karmāśaya</s>) together with its ripening,
259: And its real nature is to be understood by the examples of ‘non-friend’ and ‘cattle-footprint.’ Just as ‘non-friend’ is not merely the absence of a friend, nor merely something friend-like, but rather an enemy opposed to that; and just as a cattle-footprint is not the absence of a cattle-footprint nor merely a cattle-footprint, but a distinct entity—namely, a patch of ground other than those two; so ignorance is neither a means of valid cognition nor the absence of a means of valid cognition, but rather a different kind of cognition opposed to knowledge—this is ignorance,
260: The seeming unity of the power of the seer and the power of seeing is <s>asmitā</s> (I-notion),
262: The <s>puruṣa</s> is the power of seeing (seer-power), the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>) is the power of seeing (instrumental power); the seeming attainment of one-form-ness of these two is called the affliction (<s>kleśa</s>) ‘<s>asmitā</s>.’ When, as it were, there occurs the non-discrimination (fusion) of the enjoyer and the enjoyable powers, which are absolutely distinct and utterly unmingled, then experience (enjoyment) is contrived. But when their own nature is recovered, there is only isolation (<s>kaivalya</s>) of the two—whence, then, enjoyment? Thus it is also said—
263: “Not perceiving the <s>puruṣa</s> as distinct from the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>) by forms, dispositions, knowledge, and the like, one would, through delusion, impute self-notion there,”
265: Attachment (<s>rāga</s>) is that which accompanies pleasure,
267: For one acquainted with pleasure, that greed, craving, covetousness—preceded by the recollection of pleasure—in regard to pleasure or to its means, that is <s>rāga</s> (attachment),
268: Aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>) is that which accompanies pain,
270: For one acquainted with pain, that repulsion, resentment, desire-to-destroy, anger—preceded by the recollection of pain—in regard to pain or to its means, that is <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion),
271: Clinging-to-life (<s>abhiniveśa</s>) flows along with the taste (instinct), and is established even in the learned,
273: In all living beings there is this perpetual wish-of-the-self: “May I not cease to be; may I be again.” And this wish-of-the-self does not belong to one who has not experienced the property of death. And by this, experience in a previous birth is inferred. And this <s>abhiniveśa</s> is an affliction (<s>kleśa</s>) that flows with the native taste (instinct); the fear of death, not supportable by perception, inference, or scripture even in a newborn worm, being of the nature of a view of annihilation, makes it to be inferred that the pain of death experienced in a previous birth [now] manifests,
274: And just as this affliction is seen in the utterly deluded, so too is it established even in the learned, who know the before-and-after; why? Because in both the skillful and the unskillful alike, there is this impression from experiencing the pain of death,
275: They, subtle, are to be overcome by return-flow (<s>pratiprasava</s>)
277: Those five afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>), like seeds scorched, once dissolved in the mind of the yogin who has traversed the stages of practice, depart together with that very mind when it sets,
278: But of those that remain, having come into the state of seed-nature—
279: Their activities are to be removed by meditation (<s>dhyāna</s>)
281: The coarse activities of the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>), those which, being made thin by <s>kriyā-yoga</s>, indeed are to be abandoned by discriminative cognition (<s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>), by meditation (<s>dhyāna</s>), until they are subtilized, until they become like scorched seeds; just as, of garments, the gross dirt is first shaken off, thereafter the subtle [dirt] is removed by effort and by a means, so the coarse activities of the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) have slight opposers, whereas the subtle [activities] have great opposers,
282: The karmic deposit (<s>karmāśaya</s>), rooted in the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>), is to be experienced in seen and unseen births
284: There, the deposit of meritorious and demeritorious karma (<s>puṇya</s>-<s>apuṇya karmāśaya</s>) arises from lust, greed, delusion, anger; that one is to be experienced in a seen birth and is also to be experienced in an unseen birth. There, that which, through intense urgency, having been accomplished by mantra, austerity, and samādhi (<s>mantra</s>, <s>tapas</s>, <s>samādhi</s>), or by the propitiation of deities beginning with <s>Īśvara</s>, of great-souled ones, of great-powerful ones, is brought to perfection—that is the deposit of meritorious karma (<s>puṇya-karmāśaya</s>) which ripens immediately; likewise, the repeated injury done to those who are intensely afflicted—terrified, diseased, wretched—or to those who have attained trust, or to great-souled ones, or to ascetics, that too is the deposit of demerit (<s>pāpa-karmāśaya</s>) which ripens immediately. Thus <s>Nandīśvara</s>, the boy, having abandoned a human transformation, was transformed into a deity; likewise <s>Nahuṣa</s>, even though [becoming] the <s>Indra</s> of the gods, having abandoned his own transformation, was transformed into an animal—so it is. There, for the denizens of hell there is no deposit of karma (<s>karmāśaya</s>) to be experienced in a seen birth; and for those whose afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) are exhausted, there is also no deposit of karma to be experienced in an unseen birth,
285: When the root exists, its fruition is birth, lifespan, and experience (enjoyment-suffering)
287: When the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) are present, the deposit of karma (<s>karmāśaya</s>) undertakes (initiates) fruition, but not when the root of the afflictions has been cut off; just as rice-grains encased in husk, being of the nature of unburnt seeds, are capable of sprouting, whereas not [so] when the husk is removed or when they are of the nature of burnt seeds, so the deposit of karma, encased in afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>), becomes sprouting in fruition, not when the afflictions have been removed, not when it is of the nature of affliction-seeds scorched by discriminative cognition (<s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>), that is; and that fruition is threefold—birth, lifespan, and experience,
288: Here this is to be considered—does a single karma cause a single birth, or does a single karma propel many births? A second consideration—does many karma bring about many births, or does many karma bring about a single birth? To begin with, a single karma is not the cause of a single birth; why? Because, given the countless remainder of karma accumulated from beginningless time and also contemporary, due to the non-fixity of the order of results there would ensue for the world a lack of assurance, and that is undesirable; nor is a single karma the cause of many births; why? Because, if in many karma each single karma were the cause of many births, then the absence of a time for the remainder to ripen would ensue, and that too is undesirable; nor is many karma the cause of many births; why? Because those many births cannot occur simultaneously, and it would have to be stated that they occur only in sequence, and thus the previous defects would persist,
289: Therefore, the variegated accumulation of meritorious and demeritorious deposits of karma (<s>puṇya</s>-<s>apuṇya karmāśaya</s>) performed between birth and death, remaining with the status of principal-and-subsidiary, manifests at death, and, having been compacted into a single striking-together, brings about a swoon, produces one single birth; and that birth has a lifespan obtained by that very karma, and within that lifespan, by that very karma, experience (enjoyment-suffering) is accomplished; this deposit of karma (<s>karmāśaya</s>), being the cause of birth, lifespan, and experience, is said to have threefold fruition; therefore, a deposit of karma belonging to a single existence (one-lifetime) is stated
290: That which is to be experienced in a seen birth is a single-fruition-initiator, since it is the cause of experience (enjoyment-suffering); or, like the wind, which is a two-fruition-initiator, since it is the cause of experience—as in the case of <s>Nandīśvara</s>, and as in the case of <s>Nahuṣa</s>, thus. But through impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) that are produced by the undergoing of afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>), karma (<s>karma</s>), and fruition (<s>vipāka</s>), this mind (<s>citta</s>), condensed from beginningless time, is made variegated, as it were, being spread out everywhere like a net of fish, like being stretched with knots; these are impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) having many previous births. As for this deposit of karma (<s>karmāśaya</s>), this very one has been stated to belong to a single existence; and the formations (<s>saṃskāra</s>) that are the causes of memory (<s>smṛti</s>)—those are impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>), and they are from beginningless time
291: Now, that deposit of karma (<s>karmāśaya</s>) belonging to a single existence is of fixed fruition and of non-fixed fruition. There, for that which is to be experienced in a seen birth and has fixed fruition, this rule alone holds, not for that which is to be experienced in an unseen birth and has non-fixed fruition—why? For that which is to be experienced in an unseen birth and has non-fixed fruition, there is a threefold course: the destruction, here itself, of what has been done but has not ripened; or a descent and going-into a principal karma; or, being overpowered by a principal karma of fixed fruition, a long remaining
292: There, the destruction, here itself, of what has been done but has not ripened—just as, upon the rise of white (meritorious) karma, there is here itself the destruction of black (demeritorious) [karma]; as where this has been said—
293: “Two, two indeed, are the karmas to be understood: one heap of the evil-doer’s [acts]. The acts of the doer of merit remove that—desire, then, to perform auspicious deeds; even here the sages make known your karma,”
295: The descent and going-into a principal karma; as where this has been said—
296: “There may be a slight admixture, with remedy, with counter-consideration, not sufficient to drag down what is skillful. Why? For I have much other skillful [karma] in which this one has gone into descent; even in heaven it will make only slight diminution,”
298: Or, being overpowered by a principal karma of fixed fruition, a long remaining. How so? It has been stated that equal death is the manifesting cause for the karma which is to be experienced in an unseen birth and has fixed fruition, but not for that which is to be experienced in an unseen birth and has non-fixed fruition. Now, that karma which is to be experienced in an unseen birth and has non-fixed fruition—let it be destroyed, or let it go into descent, or, being overpowered, let it remain even a long time, so long as an equal manifesting occasion for karma does not make it face toward fruition. Because the place-time-occasion for the fruition of that [karma] is not determined, this course of karma is variegated and hard to discern. Nor is there a cessation of exceptions to the general rule; thus, the deposit of karma (<s>karmāśaya</s>) belonging to a single existence is admitted
299: Their fruits are delight and burning (pleasure and pain), since they are caused by merit and demerit (<s>puṇya</s>-<s>apuṇya</s>)
301: Those—birth, lifespan, and experience—are produced by merit in the case of the cause being merit and have pleasure as fruit, and produced by demerit in the case of the cause being demerit and have pain as fruit. And just as this pain has the nature of contrariety, so too, at the time of sense-object pleasure there certainly exists pain of a contrarious nature for the yogin
303: “Because of the pains of transformation, burning (ardor), and formation-impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>), and because of the opposition of the functions of the <s>guṇa</s>-s, all is truly pain for the discerning,”
305: For everyone, the experience of pleasure depends on means both conscious and non-conscious, pierced by attachment (<s>rāga</s>); thus there exists a deposit of karma (<s>karmāśaya</s>) born of attachment. Likewise, one hates the means of pain and is deluded—thus there also exists a deposit of karma born of aversion and delusion. And so it is said—
306: “Since enjoyment does not occur without injuring beings, therefore there also exists a bodily deposit of karma (<s>karmāśaya</s>) born of violence,”
307: thus. And sense-object pleasure has been said to be ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>)
308: That pacification (cessation) of the senses in enjoyments which is the satisfaction of the senses, that is pleasure; that non-pacification due to restlessness (greediness), that is pain. Nor can non-thirst (dispassion, <s>vaitṛṣṇyā</s>) be brought about by habituation to sense-enjoyment. Why? Because, following upon habituation to enjoyment, attachments (<s>rāga</s>-s) and the skills of the senses increase, thus. Therefore, habituation to enjoyment is not a means to pleasure. Indeed, this one, like a man afraid of a scorpion’s poison, bitten by a cobra, who, seeking pleasure, being perfumed by (steeped in) sense-objects, is sunk in a great mire of pain—this is the so-called pain-of-transformation (<s>pariṇāma-duḥkhatā</s>) which, even in a state apparently of pleasure, afflicts only the yogin,
309: Now, what is pain-of-ardor (burning, <s>tāpa-duḥkhatā</s>)? For everyone, the experience of ardor (torment) depends on means, conscious and non-conscious, pierced by aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>); thus there exists a karmic deposit (<s>karmāśaya</s>) born of aversion. And, desiring the means of pleasure, one agitates by body, speech, and mind; thereafter one benefits and injures others—thus, by benefiting and harming others one accumulates merit and demerit (<s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>). That karmic deposit arises from greed (<s>lobha</s>) and delusion (<s>moha</s>); this is what is called pain-of-ardor (<s>tāpa-duḥkhatā</s>). And what then is pain-of-formations (<s>saṃskāra-duḥkhatā</s>)? From the experience of pleasure, there is a deposit of pleasurable formations (<s>sukha-saṃskāra-āśaya</s>), and from the experience of pain, a deposit of painful formations (<s>duḥkha-saṃskāra-āśaya</s>). Thus, when, from karma, upon ripening, pleasure or pain is experienced, there is again an accumulation of karmic deposit (<s>karmāśaya</s>),
310: Thus this beginningless stream of pain, having been sent forth, perturbs the yogin alone because of its contrarious nature. Why? Because the knower is like an eye-cup (eyelid) receptacle. Just as the spider’s thread placed upon an eye-cup causes pain by touch, and not upon the other members of the body, so these pains afflict only the yogin who is like an eye-cup, not another knower. But the other, whose pain is brought on by his own karma (<s>karma</s>), taking up what is taken up, casting off what is cast off, and taking up again what is cast off, being everywhere pierced, as it were, by ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) through the manifold, beginningless impression-nature of the mind’s activities (<s>citta-vṛtti</s>), necessarily accompanies I-notion and mine-notion (<s>ahaṃkāra</s> and <s>mamakāra</s>); ever and again the threefold burns—having external, internal, and both causes—flood him. Therefore, seeing himself and the multitude of beings being buffeted by the beginningless stream of pain, the yogin takes refuge in right-seeing (<s>samyag-darśana</s>) as the means to the exhaustion of all pain,
311: And because of the opposition of the activities of the <s>guṇa</s>-s, all is truly pain for the discerning. The qualities (<s>buddhi-guṇa</s>-s), of the forms luminosity, activity, and fixity (clarity, motion, inertia), becoming mutually dependent in conferring benefit upon one another, set in motion a three-<s>guṇa</s> cognition that is serene, terrible, or stupefied. And since the activity of the <s>guṇa</s>-s is unsteady, the mind (<s>citta</s>) is said to be quickly transformed. Excess of form (intensity of a quality) and excess of activity (function) oppose one another, whereas the commonalities proceed together with the excesses. Thus these <s>guṇa</s>-s, by mutual dependence, becoming cognitions of pleasure, pain, and delusion, all become of every sort; yet their specificities are due to the predominance of a particular <s>guṇa</s>. Therefore, all is truly pain for the discerning,
312: Now, the originating seed of this great aggregate of pain is ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>), and right-seeing (<s>samyag-darśana</s>) is its cause of absence. Just as the medical science has a fourfold array—disease, cause of disease, health, remedy—so this scripture too is indeed fourfold. Namely: transmigration (<s>saṃsāra</s>), the cause of transmigration, liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>), and the means to liberation. There, the transmigration abounding in pain is to be abandoned; the conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) of <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter) and <s>puruṣa</s> (spirit) is the cause to be abandoned; the final cessation of conjunction is abandonment; the means of abandonment is right-seeing (<s>samyag-darśana</s>)
313: There, neither is the own-nature of the agent-of-abandonment to be adopted nor is it to be cast away—else, in abandoning it there would follow the fault of advocating annihilation, and in adopting it, the doctrine of causes; in denying both, there would be the doctrine of eternalism—that is right-seeing (<s>samyagdarśana</s>)
314: Accordingly, this scripture is designated as having a fourfold array—
315: What is to be abandoned is the pain that is not yet arisen
317: The past pain, having been carried beyond by enjoyment, does not fall under the side of what is to be abandoned; and the present [pain], having mounted upon enjoyment in its own moment, does not, in the next moment, come into the state of being to-be-abandoned. Therefore, that very pain which is not yet arisen afflicts the yogin, who is like an eye-cup (eyelid receptacle), and not another experiencer; that alone comes into the state of being to-be-abandoned
318: Therefore, for that very thing which is said to be to-be-abandoned, its cause is precisely indicated—
319: The conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) of the seer and the seen is the cause of what is to be abandoned
321: The seer (<s>draṣṭṛ</s>) is the <s>puruṣa</s>, the one who is re-cognizer with respect to the <s>buddhi</s>; the seen (<s>dṛśya</s>) are all dharmas mounted upon the clarity (<s>sattva</s>) of the <s>buddhi</s>. This seen, like a magnet-stone, by mere proximity renders service and, as the seen, becomes its own (belonging) of the <s>puruṣa</s>, who is of the nature of seeing and is the master, inasmuch as it comes into the condition of being the field of experience and action; though it has recovered its own nature and is independent, yet, because it is for-another, it is dependent
322: Of these two powers, the power of seeing and the power of being seen, their beginningless conjunction, caused by the object (purpose), is the cause of what is to be abandoned—the cause of pain; thus the meaning. And so it is said—“From the removal of the cause of that conjunction, there would be this absolute remedy of pain.” Why? Because one sees the remedy of that which is to be avoided, namely the cause of pain. For example—the vulnerableness-to-piercing of the sole of the foot, the thorn’s capacity-to-pierce, the avoidance is the establishing of a base for the thorn in the giving of a shoe, or the establishing of a base for the foot separated by a foot-covering; whoever in the world knows this triad, when setting about the remedy there, does not obtain the pain born of piercing. Why? Because of the capacity to apprehend the threefoldness, that is. Here too, it is the <s>sattva</s> that is heated by the heat of <s>rajas</s>. Why? Because the act of heating abides in karma; the act of heating does not abide in the field-knower (<s>kṣetrajña</s>), who is untransformed, actionless, having the domain of what has been shown; but when the <s>sattva</s> is heated, the <s>puruṣa</s>, conforming to that form, also appears to be heated
323: The own-nature of the seen is stated—
324: The seen is of the character of illumination, activity, and stability; consisting of elements and senses; for the sake of enjoyment and release (<s>apavarga</s>)
326: That whose character is illumination is <s>sattva</s>, that whose character is activity is <s>rajas</s>, that whose character is stability is <s>tamas</s>. These <s>guṇa</s>-s, mutually tinctured yet distinguished, are transformative, having the properties of conjunction and disjunction; having forms acquired through mutual dependence upon one another; though being each other’s parts and wholes, they have undisordered divisions of powers; following differences of powers that are of the same kind and of different kinds; at the time of the prominence of the <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter), having their presence shown; though being <s>guṇa</s>-s, by activity alone they are inferred to have existence as included within the <s>Pradhāna</s>; being empowered as to what is to be done for the sake of the <s>puruṣa</s>; by mere proximity, like a magnet-stone; continuing the function of any one of them without the need of a determinate cognition, they are denoted by the term <s>Pradhāna</s>. This is what is called the seen
327: This, having the nature of elements and senses (<s>bhūta</s>-<s>indriya</s>-self), transforms in the mode of elements—from earth and the rest—into subtle and gross; likewise, in the mode of senses—from ear and the rest—into subtle and gross it transforms, that is. But it does not proceed without a purpose; rather, having made the purpose prominent it proceeds—for indeed that seen (<s>dṛśya</s>) is for the sake of enjoyment and release (<s>bhoga</s>-<s>apavarga</s>) of the <s>puruṣa</s>. There, enjoyment (<s>bhoga</s>) is the ascertainment of the own-forms of desirable and undesirable qualities, fallen-into non-discrimination; release (<s>apavarga</s>) is the ascertainment of the own-form of the experiencer. Other seeing apart from these two does not exist. And thus it is said—“This indeed, when all beings, being brought under observation in the three <s>guṇa</s>-s as agents, and in the <s>puruṣa</s> as non-agent, and in the fourth as of similar and dissimilar kind, and as witnesses of those actions, are examined and found coherent, one who, not seeing, suspects another seeing,”
328: Now, these two—enjoyment and release—are wrought by the <s>buddhi</s> and subsist precisely in the <s>buddhi</s>; how are they predicated of the <s>puruṣa</s>? Just as victory or defeat, though present in the combatants, is ascribed to the lord, for he is the enjoyer of that result, so bondage and liberation, though present in the <s>buddhi</s>, are predicated of the <s>puruṣa</s>, for he is the enjoyer of that result. The non-completion of the <s>buddhi</s> itself with respect to the purpose of the <s>puruṣa</s> is bondage; the ascertainment of that purpose is liberation. By this it is indicated that grasping, retention, inference, exclusion, true-knowledge, and attachment, though present in the <s>buddhi</s>, are superimposed upon the <s>puruṣa</s> as having real being—for he is the enjoyer of that result
329: For the ascertainment of the specific-difference and own-forms of the qualities (<s>guṇa</s>-s) of the seen, this is undertaken—
330: The stages of the <s>guṇa</s>-s are the particular, the non-particular, the mere mark, and the unmarked
332: There, the five—space, air, fire, water, earth—are the elements, the particularizations of the non-particulars—the five subtle essences beginning with sound, namely sound, touch, form, taste, smell. Likewise, the ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose are the cognitive senses (<s>buddhīndriya</s>-s); speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals are the active senses (<s>karmendriya</s>-s); the eleventh is mind (<s>manas</s>), related to all objects—these are the particulars of non-particularity characterized as <s>asmitā</s> (I-ness). This is the sixteenfold particular transformation of the <s>guṇa</s>-s
333: There are six non-particulars. Namely—the subtle essence of sound, of touch, of form, of taste, and of smell: these five non-particulars, marked as one, two, three, four, five; and the sixth non-particular is mere <s>asmitā</s>. These are the six non-particular transformations of the great self (<s>mahat</s>), whose self is mere being (<s>sattā</s>-mātra). That which, from the supreme particulars, is the mere mark (<s>liṅga</s>-mātra), the great principle (<s>mahat-tattva</s>)—in that, these, abiding in mere being, in the great self, attain the limit of growth
334: And being reabsorbed, abiding in that very great self which is mere being, they apprehend that which is devoid of being-of-<s>sattva</s> and non-being-of-<s>sattva</s>, devoid of being and non-being, devoid of essence, unmanifest, unmarked (<s>aliṅga</s>), the <s>Pradhāna</s>. This is their transformation into mere mark (<s>liṅga</s>-mātra), and the transformation into the unmarked which is devoid of being-of-<s>sattva</s> and non-being-of-<s>sattva</s>
