335: In the unmarked state there is no cause of serving the purpose of the <s>puruṣa</s>; nor, in the initial unmarked state, does purposiveness for the <s>puruṣa</s> become a cause—thus there is no causing of purposiveness for it; since it does not effect the purpose of the <s>puruṣa</s>, it is called eternal. But in the three distinctive states, at the beginning, purposiveness for the <s>puruṣa</s> does become a cause; and that purpose is a cause, an occasion, a reason—therefore it is called non-eternal. But the <s>guṇa</s>-s, being concomitant with all dharmas, neither set, nor arise. Only the particulars, marked as past, future, and present, being accompanied by the <s>guṇa</s>-s, appear as if possessing the properties of production and cessation. As when one says, “Devadatta is impoverished.” Why? “Because his cows are dying”—it is from the death of the cows that he is impoverished, not from a loss of his own essential nature—such is evenness as samādhi
336: The mere mark (<s>liṅga-mātra</s>) is adjacent to the unmarked (<s>aliṅga</s>); there, each [stage], being conjoined with that [next], is to be distinguished in sequence, as the overpassings (transitions) proceed. Likewise, the six non-particulars (<s>aviśeṣa</s>-s), being conjoined in the mere mark (<s>liṅga-mātra</s>), are distinguished because of the fixity of the order of transformation; likewise, in those non-particulars, the elements-and-senses (<s>bhūta</s>-<s>indriya</s>) being conjoined are distinguished. And so it was said before: beyond the particulars there is no other principle (no further tattva); therefore, for the particulars there is no transformation into a different principle (no other-tattva transformation). But their transformations as state of property, mark of property, and condition of state (<s>dharma</s>-<s>lakṣaṇa</s>-<s>avasthā</s>-pariṇāma) will be explained
337: The seen (<s>dṛśya</s>) has been explained; now, for the purpose of ascertaining the own-form (essential nature) of the seer (<s>draṣṭṛ</s>), this is undertaken—
338: The seer is mere seeing (pure vision), though pure, he is an after-observer of cognitions (he observes cognitions)
340: “Mere seeing” means: only the power of seeing, untouched by any qualifier; that is the sense. He, the <s>puruṣa</s>, is the one who re-cognizes with respect to the <s>buddhi</s>. He is neither identical in form with the <s>buddhi</s> nor completely of different form from it. Not, to be sure, identical in form—why? Because the <s>buddhi</s> has as its domain both what is known and what is unknown, since the <s>buddhi</s> is subject to transformation; and its objects—cow and the like, or pot and the like—are both known and unknown, thus its being-transformable is shown
341: But the fact that the <s>puruṣa</s> has as his domain what is always-known (ever-known) makes manifest his non-transformability—why? For the <s>buddhi</s> cannot be said to have the <s>puruṣa</s> as its object both not-grasped and grasped; thus it is established that the <s>puruṣa</s> has as his domain what is always-known, and hence is non-transformable. Moreover, the <s>buddhi</s> is for-another (<s>parārtha</s>) because it operates as a conglomerate (is a product of conjunction); the <s>puruṣa</s> is for-self (<s>svārtha</s>). Likewise, since it determines all objects, the <s>buddhi</s> is three-<s>guṇa</s>-ed, and because of being three-<s>guṇa</s>-ed it is non-conscious; whereas the <s>puruṣa</s> is the overseer (witness) of the <s>guṇa</s>-s, therefore he is not identical in form
342: Then let him be of different form—so be it; yet he is not completely of different form—why? Because, though pure, he is an after-observer of cognitions; he after-observes the cognition that is of the <s>buddhi</s>, and by after-observing it, though he is not of that nature, he appears as if of that very nature. And so it has been said—“The power of enjoying (experiencing) is non-transformable and does not transmigrate, yet, when the transformable object is as if transmigrated (has shifted), it follows its function; and since the cognition-function of the <s>buddhi</s> has the form of having received the accession of manifested consciousness, by mere imitation of that cognition-function, the knowledge-function (in the <s>puruṣa</s>) is spoken of as not distinct from the cognition-function of the <s>buddhi</s>,”
343: The very self of the seen is for the sake of that [seer]
345: What is of the form of seeing—the <s>puruṣa</s>—when the seen has assumed the form of action (has become the domain of action), then indeed the very self of the seen is for the sake of that [seer]; that is, it becomes its own-form (essential nature) [as-for-another]. Its own-form is acquired in another’s form, when its being for enjoyment and for release (<s>bhoga</s>-<s>apavarga</s>) has been accomplished, it is not seen by the <s>puruṣa</s>; from the loss of its own-form its destruction would be imminent, yet it does not perish
347: Though destroyed with respect to the one for whom the purpose has been accomplished, it is not destroyed, because it is not common to that other (it remains common to others)
349: With respect to the one <s>puruṣa</s> whose purpose is accomplished, the seen, though destroyed (though having reached destruction), is not destroyed, because it is common to other <s>puruṣa</s>-s. With respect to a skillful (capable) <s>puruṣa</s> it has reached destruction (its purpose is done), but with respect to unskillful <s>puruṣa</s>-s it is not fulfilled; therefore, for those, the seen, having assumed the character of being the field of action, indeed attains, in another’s form, its own-form. And thus, because the powers of seeing and of being seen are eternal, their conjunction has been explained as beginningless. And so it has been said—“Because of the beginningless conjunctions of substrata (bearers of properties), even for properties alone there is a beginningless conjunction,”
350: With the intention of defining the own-nature of conjunction, this sūtra is set forth—
351: Conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>) is the cause of the apprehension of the own-forms of the power that is one’s own (self) and the power that is the owner (master)
353: The <s>puruṣa</s> (spirit), the master, is conjoined with the seen by his own [power] for the sake of seeing; therefore, from that conjunction there is the apprehension of the seen—that is enjoyment (<s>bhoga</s>), whereas the apprehension of the own-form (essential nature) of the seer—that is release (<s>apavarga</s>). The termination of the work of seeing is conjunction—that is to say, seeing is said to be the cause of disjunction; seeing is the counter-opposite of non-seeing, thus non-seeing is said to be the occasion (cause) of conjunction. Here, seeing is not the cause of liberation—since from the mere absence of non-seeing there is the absence of bondage, that is liberation. But when seeing is present, there is the destruction of non-seeing, the cause of bondage; therefore seeing—knowledge—is said to be the cause of <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation)
354: And what is this so-called non-seeing? Is it the jurisdiction (operative scope) of the <s>guṇa</s>-s, or else the non-arising of the <s>pradhāna</s>-mind (<s>pradhāna-citta</s>)—which is of the form of the seen and has its objects shown—of the master who is of the form of seeing? It is the absence of seeing when the seen is present in itself
355: What purposiveness (use) do the <s>guṇa</s>-s have? Or is it that ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>), restrained together with its own mind, is the seed of the arising of its own mind? Is it, when the formation-impressions of stability are exhausted, that the formation-impressions of motion become manifest? Where it has been said: if the <s>Pradhāna</s> abides solely in stability, then, because it does not effect transformation, it would be non-<s>Pradhāna</s>
356: Likewise, if it abides solely in motion, then, because of transformation’s being constant, it would be non-<s>Pradhāna</s>; and in both ways its operation acquires the usage (designation) “<s>Pradhāna</s>,” not otherwise. Even when other causes are posited, the same discussion applies. Some say: the very power of seeing is non-seeing, on the authority of [the scriptural statement], “
357: The activity of the <s>Pradhāna</s> is for the purpose of making known its own self,”
359: The <s>puruṣa</s>, capable of every cognition of every knowable, does not see, prior to the activity, the seen which is capable of every function and instrument; at that time it is not seen—thus. Others say: the non-seeing of both is a property (dharma). Here, then, this: even though seeing belongs to the seen as its own-self, being dependent upon the notion of the <s>puruṣa</s>, it becomes a property of the seen; likewise, even though non-seeing does not belong to the <s>puruṣa</s> as his own-self, being dependent upon the notion of the seen, it appears as if a property of the <s>puruṣa</s>. Some declare that seeing is knowledge, and non-seeing likewise. Such are the alternatives found in the scripture. Among these, this multiplicity of alternatives has as its common subject the conjunction of the <s>guṇa</s>-s with all <s>puruṣa</s>-s
360: But as for the conjunction of one whose consciousness is turned inward (<s>pratyak-cetana</s>) with his own <s>buddhi</s>—
363: That is to say, the latent impression (residual potency) of erroneous knowledge (<s>viparyaya-jñāna-vāsanā</s>). And when perfumed by the latent impression of erroneous knowledge, the <s>buddhi</s> does not attain steadfastness in the recognition of the <s>puruṣa</s> (puruṣa-discernment); being still qualified for action, it returns again. But that [same <s>buddhi</s>] attains steadfastness which culminates in recognition of the <s>puruṣa</s>; having fulfilled its task, with non-seeing ceased, and in the absence of the cause of bondage, it does not return again
364: Here someone opens [the matter] with the anecdote called “The Eunuch” (Paṇḍaka): he is addressed by his foolish wife—“O son of a eunuch, my sister is with child: for what reason, pray, am I not?” He says to her—“I am dead; I shall beget offspring,” thus. So too, this present knowledge does not effect the cessation of the mind, while [one says that] when destroyed it will do so—what expectation is that? Thereupon a teacher of the lineage says—“But surely the cessation of the <s>buddhi</s> itself is liberation; and the cessation of the <s>buddhi</s> comes about from the absence of the cause of non-seeing. And that non-seeing, the cause of bondage, is turned back by seeing. Therefore, the cessation of the mind is precisely liberation—why this confusion of judgment in a matter that is not apt?”
365: What is to be abandoned is pain, and its cause to be abandoned has been said to be conjunction, which has an occasion (cause); after this, cessation (abandonment) is to be stated—
366: From the absence of that, there is the absence of conjunction—abandonment; for that seer, <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation)
368: From the absence of that non-seeing, there is the absence of the conjunction of <s>buddhi</s> and <s>puruṣa</s>—an absolute cessation of bondage; this is the meaning. This is abandonment. <s>Kaivalya</s> (isolation) for that seer is the unmixing of the <s>puruṣa</s>, a renewed non-conjunction with the <s>guṇa</s>-s; this is the meaning. When the cause of pain has ceased, the cessation of pain is abandonment; at that time, the <s>puruṣa</s>, established in his own-form, this has been said
369: Now, what is the means of attainment for abandonment—
370: Unfaltering <s>viveka-khyāti</s> (discernment-knowledge) is the means to abandonment
372: The ascertainment that <s>sattva</s> and <s>puruṣa</s> are other (mutually distinct) is <s>viveka-khyāti</s>. And that, while false-knowledge has not ceased, wavers. When false-knowledge attains the condition of a burned seed, a barren production, then, for one whose <s>sattva</s>, with afflictions and <s>rajas</s> shaken off, abides in the supreme clarity, in the supreme mastery called subjugation, the stream of discernment-cognitions becomes stainless. That unfaltering <s>viveka-khyāti</s> is the means to abandonment. From that, there is the coming-to the state of a burned seed for false-knowledge, and further a non-production—this is the path of liberation, the means of abandonment
373: Its culminating-ground (<s>prāntabhūmi</s>) of insight is sevenfold
375: “Its” means: of the discernment just declared—this is a restatement. “Sevenfold”: when, through the removal of the impurities that are the defilements, coverings, and stains, while there is no arising of other cognitions in the mind (<s>citta</s>), the insight of the discerner (<s>vivekin</s>) is only of seven kinds
376: As follows—The to-be-abandoned is fully known; for him there is nothing to be known again as to-be-abandoned. The causes of what is to be abandoned are exhausted; there is nothing further to be exhausted for these. Abandonment has been directly realized by the samādhi of cessation. The means of abandonment in the form of <s>viveka-khyāti</s> has been cultivated. This fourfold accomplishing is the liberation with respect to insight; but the liberation of the mind (<s>citta</s>) is threefold—the <s>buddhi</s> whose entitlement to conduct has been carried through. The <s>guṇa</s>-s, like stones fallen from the edge of a mountain peak, having no foothold, heading toward dissolution into their own cause, set along with it. And for those that have dissolved, there is no re-arising again, because of the absence of purpose—so it is. In this state, beyond connection with the <s>guṇa</s>-s, pure as the mere light of his own-form, the <s>puruṣa</s> is solitary (<s>kevalī</s>). One who contemplates this sevenfold culminating insight (<s>prāntabhūmi-prajñā</s>) is called skillful (<s>kuśala</s>). Even at the reversal (return) of the <s>citta</s> into its source, he is released and indeed skillful, because he is beyond the <s>guṇa</s>-s
377: That <s>viveka-khyāti</s> is established as the means to abandonment; and there is no accomplishment without a means—this is begun—
378: From the practice of the limbs of <s>yoga</s>, with the destruction of impurity, there is the illumination of knowledge up to <s>viveka-khyāti</s>
380: The eight limbs of <s>yoga</s> are about to be stated. From their practice, there is the destruction, the annihilation, of the impurity that is of the form of error, which has five segments. Upon that destruction, there is the manifestation of right-knowledge. And the more the means are practiced, the more thinness—impurity—comes to be obtained. And as it is worn away, in correspondence with the sequence of its wearing-away, the brilliance of knowledge also increases. This growth indeed reaches the excellence of <s>viveka-khyāti</s>, up to the knowledge of the own-forms of <s>guṇa</s> and <s>puruṣa</s>—that is the meaning. The practice of the limbs of <s>yoga</s> is the cause of separation from impurity, as an axe is of what is to be cut. But it is the cause of the attainment of <s>viveka-khyāti</s>, as <s>dharma</s> is the cause of happiness, and not otherwise. And how many such causes are there in the scripture? “Only nine”—so he says. Namely—
382: Origin, continuance, manifestation, transformation, attainment by cognition; separation, otherness, and firmness are the cause, remembered ninefold
384: There, the cause of production for cognition is the mind; the cause of continuance for the mind is purposiveness-for-the-<s>puruṣa</s> (<s>puruṣārthatā</s>), just as for the body it is nourishment. The cause of manifestation is, as light is for form, so is form-cognition; the cause of transformation for the mind is a different object, as fire is for what is to be cooked. The cause by way of a ground-for-cognition (inferential sign) is smoke-cognition for fire-cognition; the cause of attainment is the practice of the limbs of <s>yoga</s> for <s>viveka-khyāti</s> (discernment-knowledge)
385: The cause of separation is that very impurity; the cause of otherness is, as for gold, the goldsmith. Likewise, for a single cognition of “woman,” ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) is [its] delusion-as-foolishness, aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>) [is its function] in the state of pain, attachment (<s>rāga</s>) in the state of pleasure, true-knowledge (<s>tattva-jñāna</s>) in neutrality. The cause of firmness is the body for the senses, and they are for it; the great elements (<s>mahābhūta</s>-s) are for bodies, and they, mutually for one another, are for all—beast, bird, human, and divine—because of being for one another’s sake. Thus there are nine causes; and these are to be applied, as the case allows, also to other categories. But the practice of the limbs of <s>yoga</s> attains a twofold causality
386: Therein the limbs of <s>yoga</s> are determined—
389: In due order we shall state their practice and their own-forms (essential definitions)
391: Non-injury (<s>ahiṃsā</s>), truth (<s>satya</s>), non-stealing (<s>asteya</s>), celibacy (<s>brahmacarya</s>), and non-acceptance (<s>aparigraha</s>) are the restraints (<s>yamāḥ</s>)
393: There, <s>ahiṃsā</s> is the non-harming of all beings in every way, at all times. And the subsequent restraints and observances (<s>yama</s> and <s>niyama</s>) have this as their root, since they are aimed at the accomplishment of this, they are taught in order to establish this; they are adopted precisely to fashion this bright-clear form. Thus it is said—“This Brāhmaṇa, in proportion as he desires to undertake many vows, turning back from negligences that cause himsa (injury) and from sources of injury, makes <s>ahiṃsā</s> of that very bright-clear form.”
394: Truth (<s>satya</s>) is speech and mind in accordance with what is real: as seen, as inferred, so are speech and mind. Speech is enjoined elsewhere for the transmission of one’s own understanding; if that should be deceitful, deluded, or barren of apprehension, then [it fails]. This is undertaken for the welfare of all beings, not for the harm of beings. And if, even so, what is spoken should be intent on the harm of beings, it would not be truth; it would be sin indeed, and by that semblance of merit, a counterfeit of merit, one would attain a grievous darkness. Therefore, having examined, one should speak truth that is for the good of all beings
395: Non-stealing (<s>asteya</s>) is the taking of others’ property without scriptural warrant; its prohibition, again, is the form of non-covetousness—thus it is <s>asteya</s>. <s>Brahmacarya</s> is the restraint of the generative organ for one whose senses are guarded. From perceiving the faults of acquisition, protection, loss, attachment, and injury with respect to objects, not accepting—this is <s>aparigraha</s>. These are the restraints (<s>yamāḥ</s>)
397: Not delimited by class, place, time, or occasion—they are universal, the great vow
399: There, <s>ahiṃsā</s> delimited by class is, for a fisherman, only with regard to fish and not otherwise injury; the same delimited by place is, “I will not kill at a sacred ford”; the same delimited by time is, “Not on the fourteenth, not on an auspicious day will I kill”; the same delimited by convention for one who has refrained by these three is, “For the sake of gods or Brāhmaṇas, and not otherwise, will I kill.” And as for Kṣatriyas, injury is only in battle and not otherwise. But not delimited by these—class, place, time, and convention—<s>ahiṃsā</s> and the rest are to be observed absolutely in every way. Because they are to be known as without any transgression anywhere, in all domains and in every way, they are called universal, the great vow
400: Purity (<s>śauca</s>), contentment (<s>saṃtoṣa</s>), austerity (<s>tapas</s>), recitation-and-study (<s>svādhyāya</s>), and dedication to the Lord (<s>īśvara-praṇidhāna</s>) are the observances (<s>niyamāḥ</s>)
402: There, purity (<s>śauca</s>) external is produced by rubbing with water and the like, and includes the taking of what is clean (pure) as food, and so on; internal is the washing away of the stains of the mind (<s>citta</s>). Contentment (<s>saṃtoṣa</s>) is the non-coveting of what is beyond the means at hand. Austerity (<s>tapas</s>) is the endurance of the pairs of opposites; and the pairs are hunger and thirst, cold and heat, standing and sitting, the wooden-vow silence and the form-vow silence. And the vows for these, according to fitness, are the <s>kṛcchra</s>, <s>cāndrāyaṇa</s>, <s>sāṃtapana</s>, and the like. Recitation-and-study (<s>svādhyāya</s>) is the study of the scriptures concerning liberation, or else the muttered repetition of the <s>praṇava</s> (om). Dedication to the Lord (<s>īśvara-praṇidhāna</s>) is the offering of all actions unto Him, the supreme teacher
403: Lying on a bed, or seated, or then traveling on a path, or being at ease in oneself, one whose net of deliberations has been worn away,
404: beholding the exhaustion of the seed of transmigration (<s>saṃsāra</s>), would be constantly yoked (steadfast), a partaker of the enjoyment of the deathless (nectar)
405: Where this has been said: from that there is also the attainment of inward-turned consciousness (<s>pratyak-cetanā</s>), and the absence of obstacles
406: For these restraints and observances (<s>yama</s> and <s>niyama</s>)—
407: When there is disturbance by contrary deliberations (<s>vitarka</s>), there is the cultivation of the opposite (counter-reflection) (<s>pratipakṣa-bhāvanā</s>)
409: When, for this Brāhmaṇa, deliberations such as injury arise—“I shall kill the wrongdoer; I shall even speak falsehood; I shall take even his property; and with respect to his wives I shall engage in intercourse; and with respect to his possessions I shall become the master”—thus, being afflicted by the fever of deliberations that are bent on a wrong path, blazing exceedingly, he should cultivate their opposites. “I, being cooked in the terrible embers of <s>saṃsāra</s>, have taken refuge: by granting fearlessness to all beings is the <s>yoga</s>-duty.” And, “I indeed, having abandoned deliberations, if I again take them up, am like one of a dog’s behavior”—so let him reflect; “Just as a dog licks up its vomit, so is the taking up again of what has been abandoned.” The like should be applied also in other sūtra-passages
410: Deliberations—injury and the rest—done, caused to be done, or approved, preceded by greed, anger, and delusion, mild, middling, or intense, have suffering, ignorance, and endlessness as their fruit—this is the counter-reflection (<s>pratipakṣa-bhāvanā</s>)
412: There, as to injury first: “done, caused to be done, approved” is threefold; and each single one is again threefold—by greed, “for the sake of flesh, hide, or wealth”; by anger, “this one has wronged me”; by delusion, “merit will accrue to me.” And greed, anger, and delusion are again threefold—mild, middling, intense; thus there are twenty-seven varieties of injury. The mild, middling, and intense are again threefold—mild-of-mild, middling-of-mild, intense-of-mild; likewise, mild-of-middling, middling-of-middling, intense-of-middling; likewise, mild-of-intense, middling-of-intense, intense-of-intense. Thus injury becomes of eighty-one varieties. And further, because of the differentiations by the alternatives, combinations, and accumulations of observances (<s>niyama</s>), it is incalculable, since the differentiation of living beings is innumerable—thus. The same is to be applied, as fits, also to falsehood and the rest
413: Indeed, those deliberations have suffering, ignorance, and endlessness as their fruit—this is the counter-reflection: those whose fruit is suffering, ignorance, and endlessness. And thus, the injurer, to begin with, strikes down the strength of the one to be slain; then, by the fall of weapon and the like, he causes suffering; then he releases him even from life. Then, because of that striking down of strength, the sentient and insentient instruments of the injurer become of diminished vigor. Producing suffering, he experiences suffering in hell, animal, ghost, and the like; and, because he has removed another’s opportunity for living, at every moment, being in the vicinity of the end of life, wishing even for death, he barely draws breath, since the experiencing of the ripening of suffering is bound to its fixed ripening. And if, by some means, injury be attended by the fading of merit, then, upon the attainment of pleasure there, he would be of short life—thus. The same is to be applied, as possible, also to falsehood and the rest. Thus, reflecting that the ripening that follows these deliberations is undesirable, one should not place the mind upon deliberations
414: From the cultivation of the counter-reflection (<s>pratipakṣa-bhāvanā</s>), as the cause, the deliberations (<s>vitarka</s>) are to be abandoned; when for him they have the character of non-production, then the mastery produced by that becomes for the <s>yogin</s> an indication of attainment (success); for example—
415: When non-injury (<s>ahiṃsā</s>) is established, in its vicinity hostility is relinquished,
418: When truth (<s>satya</s>) is established, there is reliance on the fruit of action,
420: namely, “Let him become righteous”—thus he becomes righteous; “Let him obtain heaven”—thus he obtains heaven; or his speech becomes unfailing
421: When non-stealing (<s>asteya</s>) is established, there is the presence of all jewels,
423: the jewels from all quarters come and attend upon him
424: When celibacy (<s>brahmacarya</s>) is established, there is the acquisition of vigor (<s>vīrya</s>),
426: by the acquisition of which, unobstructed, he enhances the qualities (<s>guṇa</s>-s); and, being accomplished, he becomes capable of establishing knowledge in disciples
427: With firmness in non-acceptance (<s>aparigraha</s>) there is knowledge of the how of birth,
429: there arises for him the inquiry into the state of the self in its own nature, across the prior-end, the later-end, and the middle, namely: “Who was I? how was I? what is this? how indeed is this? who shall we be? and how shall we be?” These are the attainments upon firmness in the restraints (<s>yama</s>)
430: As to the observances (<s>niyama</s>), we shall state—
431: From purity (<s>śauca</s>) there is disgust toward one’s own limbs, and non-contact with others,
433: When there is disgust toward one’s own body, one, commencing purity, becomes a renunciant who sees the defects of the body and is not attached to the body. Moreover, as for non-contact with others: seeing the nature of the body, wishing to abandon even one’s own body, even while washing it with clay, water, and the like, not perceiving purity of the body—how would he be joined in an extreme way, and effortlessly, with others’ bodies?
435: Clarity of <s>sattva</s> (purity of the mind-stuff), cheerfulness, one-pointedness, mastery of the senses, and fitness for the vision of the self,
437: are obtained—thus is the completion of the sentence. From purity there is purity of <s>sattva</s>; from that, cheerfulness; from that, one-pointedness; from that, mastery of the senses; and from that, fitness of the <s>buddhi</s>-<s>sattva</s> for the vision of the self—this is attained from steadiness in purity
438: From contentment (<s>saṃtoṣa</s>) there is the acquisition of unsurpassed happiness,
442: Whatever pleasure of desire there is in the world, and whatever great divine happiness,
443: these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the happiness of the extinction of thirst (craving),
445: Perfection of body and senses comes from austerity (<s>tapas</s>) through the destruction of impurity,
447: Austerity, even while being undertaken, destroys the impurity that is a covering-filth; from the removal of that covering-filth there is perfection of the body, beginning with minuteness (<s>aṇimā</s>) and the rest. Likewise there is perfection of the senses—hearing and seeing from afar, and so on
448: From recitation-and-study (<s>svādhyāya</s>) there is connection with the desired deity,
450: the gods, the seers, and the accomplished ones (<s>siddha</s>-s) come into the sight of one devoted to recitation-and-study, and they also engage with him in his undertaking
451: Perfection of <s>samādhi</s> comes from dedication to the Lord (<s>īśvara-praṇidhāna</s>),
453: for one whose entire being is offered to the Lord, there is the perfection of <s>samādhi</s>, by which he knows truly all that is desired—without falsehood—across another place, another body, and another time; then his discernment knows things as they actually are
454: The restraints and observances (<s>yama</s> and <s>niyama</s>) have been stated together with their attainments; we shall state the postures and the rest. There—
457: for example: <s>padmāsana</s>, <s>bhadrāsana</s>, <s>svastika</s>, <s>daṇḍāsana</s>, with support, couch-seated (<s>paryaṅka</s>), heron-seated (<s>krauñca-niṣadana</s>), elephant-seated (<s>hasti-niṣadana</s>), camel-seated (<s>uṣṭra-niṣadana</s>), equal-poise (<s>sama-saṃsthāna</s>), firm-comfortable, and as-pleasing—thus and the like
458: By the relaxation of effort and by samāpatti upon the infinite,
460: —so is the completion of the sentence—posture is perfected by the cessation of effort, whereby there is no shaking of the limbs; or, when the mind is absorbed in the Infinite, it brings posture to completion
461: Then there is non-affliction by the pairs of opposites,
463: by mastery of posture one is not overcome by the pairs beginning with cold and heat
464: When that is present, regulation of the movement of inhalation and exhalation is breath-control (<s>prāṇāyāma</s>)
466: As part of the attainment of posture (<s>āsana-jaya</s>), the sipping-in of the external air is inhalation (<s>śvāsa</s>), and the expelling of the cavity’s air is exhalation (<s>praśvāsa</s>); the cessation of movement of these two, or the absence of both, is <s>prāṇāyāma</s> (regulation of the movement of inhalation and exhalation)
468: Has the form of external, internal, and retention functions, observed by place, time, and number, being long and subtle
470: That in which there is absence of movement preceded by exhalation is the external (pause); that in which there is absence of movement preceded by inhalation is the internal (pause). The third is the retention-function, wherein the absence of both occurs from a single exertion. Just as water placed on a heated stone shrinks together on all sides, so there is the simultaneous absence of movement of both. All these three are observed by place: “this much is its sphere, namely place”; they are observed by time, meaning delimited by the determination of the measure of instants; they are observed by number, namely: by this many inhalations and exhalations the first uplift (cycle), likewise, with them restrained by this many, the second uplift; and thus the third. In this way—mild, thus medium, thus intense—so it is observed by number. This indeed, practiced thus, becomes long and subtle
471: A fourth (prāṇāyāma) is that which projects (or extends) the external and internal objects (ranges) [i.e., spheres] of operation
473: Observed by place, time, and number with respect to the external sphere, it is extended; likewise, observed with respect to the internal sphere, it is extended; in both ways it is long and subtle. Preceded by that, from mastery of the stage (<s>bhūmi-jaya</s>) there is, progressively, the absence of movement of both—this is the fourth <s>prāṇāyāma</s>. But the third is the absence of movement not considering the objects (i.e., without fixing the spheres), once undertaken, and it is observed by place, time, and number—long and subtle; whereas the fourth, from the determination of the objects of inhalation and exhalation, and through progressive mastery of the stages, is an absence of movement preceded by the extension of both (spheres)—this is the specificity
474: Then the covering of the light is thinned
476: For this yogin who practices <s>prāṇāyāma</s>, the karma that veils discriminative knowledge (<s>viveka-jñāna</s>) is attenuated. This they describe: with an illusory net made of great delusion it covers the luminous <s>sattva</s> (clarity-nature) and appoints it to what ought not to be done; that karma is his light-covering, the bond of <s>saṃsāra</s> (cycle of rebirth). That property which is immediately subsequent to a given property is its sequence. “The lump perishes, the pot arises”—this is the sequence of transformation by property. 596: Karma is with-commencement and without-commencement; from <s>saṃyama</s> on that, knowledge of the end of another’s life, or from portents (<s>ariṣṭa</s>)
598: Karma that yields lifespan-result is twofold: with-commencement and without-commencement. Therein, just as a wet cloth, having been spread out, would dry in a shorter time, so is the with-commencement; and just as that very cloth, when tightly wrung together, would dry only after a long time, so is the without-commencement. And just as fire, set in a dry thicket and joined on all sides with wind, would burn in a shorter time, so is the with-commencement; and just as that same fire, placed successively upon the parts in a heap of grass, would burn only after a long time, so is the without-commencement. Therefore the karma that produces lifespan in a single birth is twofold, with-commencement and without-commencement; from <s>saṃyama</s> (the combined practice of <s>dhāraṇā</s>, <s>dhyāna</s>, and <s>samādhi</s>) on that, there is knowledge of the end of another’s departure (death)
599: Or from portents (<s>ariṣṭa</s>): the <s>ariṣṭa</s> are threefold—pertaining to the self (<s>ādhyātmika</s>), pertaining to beings/elements (<s>ādhibhautika</s>), and pertaining to deities (<s>ādhidaivika</s>). There, the <s>ādhyātmika</s> is: one does not hear a sound in one’s own body when the ear is covered, or one does not see light in the eye though it is steady; likewise, the <s>ādhibhautika</s>: one sees the messengers of <s>Yama</s>, one sees ancestors (<s>pitṛ</s>-s) who have passed away, unexpectedly; likewise, the <s>ādhidaivika</s>: one sees heaven unexpectedly, or <s>siddha</s>-s; or all is inverted—by this he knows that the end (death) has approached

619: There, in <s>Pātāla</s>, in the ocean, in the mountains, in these places, the classes of gods reside—<s>Asura</s>, <s>Gandharva</s>, <s>Kiṃnara</s>, <s>Kiṃpuruṣa</s>, <s>Yakṣa</s>, <s>Rākṣasa</s>, <s>Bhūta</s>, <s>Preta</s>, <s>Piśāca</s>, <s>Apasmāraka</s>, <s>Apsaras</s>, <s>Brahmarākṣasa</s>, <s>Kūṣmāṇḍa</s>, and <s>Vināyaka</s>; on all the continents dwell virtuous ones—gods and humans
620: <s>Sumeru</s> is the garden-ground of the Thirty-three (<s>Tridaśa</s>); there are the groves <s>Miśravaṇa</s>, <s>Nandana</s>, <s>Caitraratha</s>, and <s>Sumānasa</s>, such are the parks; <s>Sudharmā</s> is the divine assembly-hall, <s>Sudarśana</s> the city; <s>Vaijayanta</s> the palace; the planets, lunar mansions, and stars are fastened to <s>Dhruva</s>, their courses observed by the regulation of the casting by wind, and, positioned one above another over <s>Sumeru</s>, they revolve in the sky
621: The six classes of gods dwelling in the <s>Māhendra</s> (heaven) are—the <s>Tridaśa</s>, the <s>Agniṣvātta</s>, the <s>Yāmya</s>, the <s>Tuṣita</s>, the <s>Aparinirmitavaśavartin</s>, and the <s>Parinirmitavaśavartin</s>; all accomplish by mere resolve, endowed with the lordly powers beginning with <s>aṇimā</s> (minuteness), having the lifespan of an aeon, attendant youths, enjoyers of sense-pleasures, with spontaneously produced bodies, and waited upon by <s>Apsaras</s> of supremely agreeable forms
622: In the great world of <s>Prajāpati</s>, there is a fivefold class of gods—<s>Kumuda</s>, <s>Ṛbhava</s>, <s>Pratardana</s>, <s>Añjanābhā</s>, and <s>Pracitābhā</s>; these hold sway over the great elements (<s>mahābhūta</s>), take meditation as their food, and have lifespans of a thousand aeons. In the first, in the world of <s>Brahmā</s> called <s>Jana</s>, there is a fourfold class of gods—<s>Brahmapurohita</s>-s, <s>Brahmakāyika</s>-s, <s>Brahmamahākāyika</s>-s, and the <s>Amara</s>-s; they hold sway over the elements-and-senses (<s>bhūta</s>-<s>indriya</s>) and have lifespans that are successively doubled upon being doubled
623: In the second, in the world of <s>Tapas</s>, there is a threefold class of gods—<s>Ābhāsvara</s>, <s>Mahābhāsvara</s>, and <s>Satyamahābhāsvara</s>; they hold sway over elements, senses, and <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature), all have lifespans successively doubled upon being doubled, subsist on meditation, are upward-viriled (<s>ūrdhvaretas</s>), unimpeded in knowledge upwards, and in the lower levels their fields of knowledge are not veiled. In the third, in the world of <s>Brahmā</s> called <s>Satya</s>, there are four classes of gods, who have not undertaken the establishment of abodes, having their own foundation, situated higher and higher, holding sway over <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter), with lifespans that last as long as a creation-cycle
624: There, the <s>Acyuta</s>-s enjoy the bliss of <s>savitaraka-dhyāna</s> (discernment-with-thought meditation); the <s>Śuddhanivāsa</s>-s enjoy the bliss of <s>savicāra-dhyāna</s> (reflection-with-inquiry meditation); the <s>Satyābhā</s>-s enjoy the bliss of meditation consisting solely of bliss (<s>ānandamātra-dhyāna</s>); and the <s>Saṃjñāsaṃjñin</s>-s enjoy the bliss of meditation consisting solely of <s>asmitā</s> (I-am-ness). These too stand established in the midst of the three worlds. These are the seven worlds, all indeed the worlds of <s>Brahmā</s>. But those of disembodiedness and dissolution-into-<s>Prakṛti</s> (<s>videha</s> and <s>prakṛtilaya</s>) operate on the path of liberation, therefore they are not placed within the midst of the worlds. This should be directly realized by the yogin, having performed <s>saṃyama</s> on the gate of the sun; thereafter, elsewhere too, let him so practice until this entire [cosmos] has been seen
625: From [<s>saṃyama</s> on] the moon, knowledge of the array of stars

628: From [<s>saṃyama</s> on] <s>Dhruva</s> (the Pole Star), knowledge of their motion
630: Then, having performed <s>saṃyama</s> on <s>Dhruva</s>, one should discern the movement of the stars; having performed <s>saṃyama</s> on the aerial vehicles above, one should discern those

634: In the throat-pit, the cessation of hunger and thirst

640: In the light at the crown, the sight of <s>Siddha</s>-s

646: In the heart, awareness of mind (<s>citta</s>)
648: That which here, in this city of <s>Brahman</s>, is the small lotus-like abode—there is cognition; from <s>saṃyama</s> on that, there is awareness of the mind (<s>citta-saṃvit</s>)

651: The luminosity of intellect (<s>buddhi-sattva</s>) has the character of manifestness; when bound together with a substratum of like-<s>sattva</s>, having subdued rajas and tamas, it is transformed with the cognition of the otherness of <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>. 657: From <s>Prātibha</s>, knowledge of the subtle, the interveningly remote, the far-off, the past, and the future; from clairaudience, the hearing of divine sounds; from tactile-cognition, attainment of divine touch; from visionary-seeing, knowledge of divine forms; from exquisite taste, knowledge of divine flavors; from report, knowledge of divine scents—these arise continually
658: These are impediments in <s>samādhi</s>, and perfections (<s>siddhi</s>-s) in emergence (from absorption)
660: These, beginning with <s>Prātibha</s>, arising for one whose mind (<s>citta</s>) is collected in <s>samādhi</s>, are impediments, because they are opposed to the vision (of truth); arising for one whose mind is emergent, they are <s>siddhi</s>-s
661: From the loosening of the cause of bondage and from knowledge of the course (movement) of the mind, there is entry of the mind into another’s body
663: The binding—namely the establishment of the mind, which has become unsteady and ungrounded in the body—occurs by the power of the deposit of karma; the slackening of that, the cause of bondage—of that karma—takes place through the power of <s>samādhi</s>. 664: From the mastery of <s>Udāna</s> (the upward-breath), non-contact with water, mud, thorns, and the like, and also ascension (at death)
666: The entire operation of the senses, characterized as the breaths beginning with <s>Prāṇa</s>, is life; its functions are fivefold: <s>Prāṇa</s> has the course in the mouth and nose, its activity being toward the heart; from distributing equally, <s>Samāna</s>, with activity in the navel; from moving downward, <s>Apāna</s>, with activity in the soles of the feet; from moving upward, <s>Udāna</s>, with activity in the head; all-pervading is <s>Vyāna</s>. Among these, the chief is <s>Prāṇa</s>. From the mastery of <s>Udāna</s> there is non-contact with water, mud, thorns, and the like, and also ascension at the time of departure (death); he attains that as lordship (control)
667: From the mastery of <s>Samāna</s>, kindling (of fire)
669: One who has conquered <s>Samāna</s>, having performed fanning of the fire by heat, causes it to blaze
670: From <s>saṃyama</s> on the connection of the ear and space (<s>ākāśa</s>), divine hearing
672: For the support of all ears is <s>ākāśa</s>, and so too of all sounds, as has been said—because, when sounds are heard in the same place, there is the hearing of a single locality for them all—this is the mark of <s>ākāśa</s>
673: And its non-obstruction has been stated; likewise, from the seeing of the non-obstruction of the formless, the all-pervasiveness of <s>ākāśa</s> is well-known. For the yogin who has performed <s>saṃyama</s> on the connection of ear and <s>ākāśa</s>, divine hearing proceeds
674: From <s>saṃyama</s> on the connection of body and space, and from attainment of lightness like that of cotton, movement through <s>ākāśa</s> (space)
676: Where the body is, there is space, by its granting an opening (room) to the body; by that, there is the body’s connection with it.
