677: External, non-conceptual operation—[that is] the great incorporeality (<s>mahā-videha</s>); from that, the destruction of the covering of light
679: Outside the body, the obtaining of a mental operation—this concentration is called ‘incorporeal’ (<s>videhā</s>); if that occurs for a mind established in the body merely as an external operation, it is said to be constructed (imagined), whereas the external operation of a mind that is in fact external, independent of the body, that indeed is unconstructed; by means of the constructed one they accomplish the unconstructed great incorporeality (<s>mahā-videhā</s>). By that, yogins enter other bodies; and from that concentration, the triple covering of the luminosity-nature of the intellect (<s>buddhi-sattva</s>)—defilements, karmas, and their ripenings, whose root is rajas and tamas—there is the cessation of that covering.
680: From <s>saṃyama</s> on grossness, essential-nature, subtlety, conjunction (anvaya), and meaningfulness (arthavattva), mastery over the elements (<s>bhūta</s>-s)
682: Therein, the particular qualities beginning with sound and so on pertaining to earth and the rest, along with properties such as co-operation (mutual assistance), are designated by the term ‘gross’; this is the first form of the elements. The second form is their own generality, their essential-nature: solidity is earth, liquidity is water, heat is fire, motion is wind, all-pervasiveness is space—this is what is called by the term ‘essential-nature’.
683: Of this generality, the particular qualities beginning with sound and so on [are its differentiations]; thus it is said: ‘For those endowed with one genus, the mere exclusion by way of properties [marks out their differences].’
684: Here, the aggregation of generality and particularity is substance (dravya). A group rests in two ways: following (pervading) members whose differences are suppressed—‘body,’ ‘tree,’ ‘troop,’ ‘forest’, thus.
685: A group that follows members whose differences have been grasped by a word—‘both gods and humans’; of the group, gods are one part, humans a second part; by these two the group itself is denoted.
686: And it is spoken of with difference or non-difference intended: ‘a grove of mango trees,’ ‘an assembly of <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>-s’—‘a mango-grove,’ ‘a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>-assembly’, thus.
687: And further, it is twofold: having conjointly accomplished parts (yuta-siddha-avayava) and having non-conjointly accomplished parts (ayuta-siddha-avayava). A group with conjointly accomplished parts is ‘forest,’ ‘assembly’; with non-conjointly accomplished parts it is ‘aggregate,’ ‘body,’ ‘tree,’ ‘atom.’ ‘A group that follows divisions of non-conjointly accomplished parts is substance’—so says <s>Patañjali</s>; this was stated as the essential-nature.
688: Now, what is their subtle form? The <s>tanmātra</s>-s, the causes of the elements; of that, a single part is the atom (<s>paramāṇu</s>); an aggregation that follows divisions whose nature is generality-and-particularity and non-conjointly accomplished parts; in this way, all the <s>tanmātra</s>-s—this is the third [form]. Next, the fourth form of the elements is the qualities (<s>guṇa</s>-s) of manifestation, activity, stability—following their functional natures—which are indicated by the term ‘conjunction’ (anvaya). Next, their fifth form is meaningfulness (arthavattva), the being-for-experience-and-release (enjoyment and emancipation), which inheres indeed in the <s>guṇa</s>-s; and the <s>guṇa</s>-s in the subtle, elemental, and gross composites—thus all is meaningful. Now, from <s>saṃyama</s> on these five elements in their five forms, there arises the seeing of the essential-nature of each respective form, and mastery. There, having conquered the five essential-natures of the elements, one becomes a master of the elements; by that mastery, the elemental natures become obedient to his resolve, like cows following their calves.
689: Then the manifestation of the powers beginning with minuteness (<s>aṇimā</s>), perfection of the body, and non-impediment by the properties of that [body]
691: Therein, <s>aṇimā</s> is ‘he becomes minute like an atom’; lightness (<s>laghimā</s>) is ‘he becomes light’; greatness (<s>mahimā</s>) is ‘he becomes great.’ ‘Reach’ (<s>prāpti</s>) is: with even a fingertip he touches the moon. ‘Pervasion’ (<s>prākāmya</s>) is the non-impediment of will—on earth he emerges and submerges as in water. ‘Mastery’ (<s>vaśitva</s>) is: he becomes lord over elemental and composite things; and ‘lordship’ (<s>īśitṛtva</s>) over their productions, dissolutions, and arrangements is desired. Where there is determination according to desire (<s>kāmāvasāyitva</s>), there is truth of resolve: just as the resolve, so the state of the elemental natures. Nor, though capable, does he effect a reversal of the categories—why? Because for another who has the determination according to desire previously accomplished, thus the arrangement of the elements is by his resolve. These are the eight <s>aiśvarya</s>-s (lordly powers).
692: The perfection of the body will be stated—non-impediment by its properties as well: the earth-nature does not confine the yogin’s bodily actions such as entering even a rock; waters, though unctuous, do not moisten; fire, though hot, does not burn; wind, though impelling, does not carry away; even in <s>ākāśa</s> (space), whose nature is non-obstruction, he becomes one whose body is veiled, he becomes invisible even to <s>Siddha</s>-s
693: Beauty of form, loveliness, strength, and adamantine compactness are the perfection of the body
695: He is handsome to behold, radiant, possessed of exceptional strength, and of adamantine compactness
696: From <s>saṃyama</s> on apprehension, essential-form, egoity (<s>asmitā</s>), conjunction (anvaya), and meaningfulness (arthavattva), there is mastery over the senses
698: What is to be apprehended—sound and the rest—whose nature is generality-and-particularity, this is the grāhya; the operation of the senses upon those is apprehension. And not, with respect to that, would the mind subsequently determine a particular object, when the sense has apprehended a mere generality without having attended to it—how so? The essential-form, further, of the luminosity-nature of the intellect (<s>buddhi-sattva</s>) is the sense-organ as substance (dravya), a collection that follows the divisions of non-conjointly accomplished parts of generality and particularity. Their third form is <s>asmitā</s>-characterized <s>ahaṃkāra</s> (ego-maker); of that generality, the senses are the particularizations. The fourth form is the <s>guṇa</s>-s, whose nature is determination, illumination-activity-stability; the senses are transformations of that <s>ahaṃkāra</s>. The fifth form is the being-for-the-<s>Puruṣa</s>-purpose (<s>puruṣārthavattva</s>) that inheres in the <s>guṇa</s>-s. From <s>saṃyama</s>, in due order, on these five forms of the senses, having effected mastery there in each place, from the conquest of the five forms there arises for the yogin mastery of the senses
699: Then, speed like the mind, the state of being without organs, and mastery of <s>Pradhāna</s>
701: The unsurpassed attainment of speed for the body is speed like the mind. The state of being without organs is the attainment of operations by the disembodied senses, with reference to the desired place, time, and object. Mastery of all modifications of <s>Prakṛti</s> (all nature’s evolutes) is mastery of <s>Pradhāna</s>; these three perfections are called the honey-symbol, and these are attained from mastery of the fivefold forms of the instruments (senses)
702: Of mere knowledge of the otherness of <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>, lordship over all entities and omniscience
704: When the luminosity of intellect (<s>buddhi-sattva</s>), its rajas and tamas shaken off, abides in the highest clarity, in that state called mastery (vaśīkāra), established in the mere form of knowledge of the otherness of <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>, there is lordship over all entities—meaning: the <s>guṇa</s>-s, being universal, of the nature of determination and determinables, present themselves to the Lord, the Knower-of-the-field (<s>kṣetrajña</s>), as nothing but the seen. Omniscience is discriminative knowledge, not proceeding in sequence, of the <s>guṇa</s>-s as universal, established with the properties of quiescent, arisen, and inexpressible; this is the siddhi named ‘free from sorrow,’ by attaining which the yogin, having his afflictions and bonds worn away, dwells as a master
705: From dispassion toward that too, through the destruction of the seed of defects, <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation) [ensues]
707: When for him it is thus—the afflictions and karma having been destroyed—this dharma of discriminative discernment of <s>sattva</s> arises, and <s>sattva</s> is consigned to the category to-be-abandoned, while <s>Puruṣa</s>, unchanging, pure, other than <s>sattva</s>, thus; accordingly, as he becomes dispassionate toward that, whatever seeds of afflictions there are, like burnt rice-grains, incapable of sprouting, these, together with the mind, go away, having been cast aside. When these are dissolved, the <s>Puruṣa</s> no longer experiences this triple suffering. Then, when the <s>guṇa</s>-s—manifest in the mind in the form of karma, afflictions, and their ripenings—have fulfilled their purpose and reabsorb, the absolute disconnection of the <s>Puruṣa</s> from the <s>guṇa</s>-s is <s>kaivalya</s>; then the power of awareness, established in its own nature, is the <s>Puruṣa</s> alone
708: When invited in high places, the non-production of attachment and pride, because of the recurrence of undesired consequences
710: Indeed, these four yogins are as follows: the beginner on the path (prāthamakalpika), the one whose ground is honey-like (madhubhūmika), the one whose light is wisdom (prajñājyotis), and the one who has gone beyond what is to be cultivated (atikrāntabhāvanīya); among these, the practitioner (abhyāsin), whose light has just been set in motion, is the first, the one whose knowledge bears truth (<s>ṛtaṃbhara-prajñā</s>) is the second, the conqueror of elements and senses (bhūtendriyajayī) is the third—having secured protection-bonds in all matters that have been cultivated, in what is to be cultivated, these means are to be undertaken; but the fourth, who indeed has gone beyond what is to be cultivated, for him the re-production of the mind (citta-pratisarga) has the single purpose, and his knowledge of the terminal grounds (prānta-bhūmi-prajñā) is sevenfold
711: There, when the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> who directly realizes the honeyed ground is seen by the stationed gods, perceiving the purification of his <s>sattva</s>, they invite him from their stations: ‘Come, dwell here, enjoy yourself here; this enjoyment is delightful, this maiden is delightful, this elixir cures old age and death, this is an aerial vehicle; these are wish-fulfilling trees (<s>kalpadruma</s>-s); the sacred <s>Mandākinī</s>; perfected beings and great seers, supreme; the <s>Apsaras</s>-es are favorable; divine ears and eyes; a body like adamant; all this has been acquired by your own virtues; O long-lived one, obtain this imperishable, ageless, immortal station, dear to the gods’—thus; being thus addressed, he should reflect upon the faults of attachment, ‘While the embers of <s>saṃsāra</s> are horrible, I have been roasted; in the darkness of birth-and-death I have been tossed about; somehow attained by me is the lamp of yoga, which destroys the darkness of the afflictions, and these, the winds of objects, sources of thirst (craving), are its opposites; indeed, having obtained the light, how would I be deceived by this mirage of objects? Should I again make myself the fuel of the blazing fire of <s>saṃsāra</s> itself?’—‘Blessings upon you, O sense-objects, akin to dreams, pitiable, things to be begged for by the wretched’—with his mind thus firmly decided, he should cultivate <s>samādhi</s>
712: Without forming attachment, he should not even make self-pleasing pride; thinking, ‘Thus am I one to be besought even by the gods,’ out of such pride, with the complacency of being well-established, he will not consider himself as being, as it were, seized by death by the hair; and accordingly, since lapses and openings are ever to be watched for with diligent care, negligence, having obtained a gap, will prop up the afflictions, then there follows again an undesired consequence; thus, for him who does not make attachment and pride, what has been cultivated will be made firm, and the object to be cultivated will incline into nearness
713: From <s>saṃyama</s> on instants and their sequence, knowledge born of discrimination (vivekaja) [arises]
715: Just as, up to the limit of diminution, a substance is an atom, so up to the limit of utmost diminution, time is an instant; inasmuch as, within whatever time a <s>paramāṇu</s> (atom) having moved would abandon its former place and attain the subsequent place—that is time, the instant; the uninterrupted flow of that is sequence; there is no aggregation of things of instants and of their sequence, thus the aggregation is of cognitions: muhūrtas, days-and-nights, and the like; this time indeed, though devoid of thinghood, is constructed by cognition, accompanied by sound and knowledge, and to those whose view is worldly, arisen from emergence, it appears as though it were the very nature of things
716: An instant (kṣaṇa), when fallen upon a substance, relies on sequence; and sequence has the nature of the immediate succession of instants—this the knowers of time, the <s>yogin</s>-s, designate as time. Nor do two instants exist together, and there is no sequence of two that co-exist, because co-existence is impossible; the immediacy of the subsequent-becoming with respect to the prior—this immediacy of the instant is sequence; therefore only the present instant alone exists, not past and future instants. Hence, there is no aggregation of that; but the instants that are past and future are to be explained as accompanied by transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>); by that single instant, the entire world undergoes transformation. Indeed, all properties (dharmas) mount upon that very instant; from <s>saṃyama</s> on those two—on the instant and on that sequence—there is direct realization of the two; and then knowledge born of discrimination (<s>vivekaja jñāna</s>) appears
717: A particular domain of that is briefly presented—
718: From the non-limitation by difference of genus (jāti), mark (lakṣaṇa), and place (deśa), in two that are alike, there is apprehension (pratipatti) from that
720: When two are alike in place, mark, and essential-form, difference of genus is the cause of otherness: “this is a cow, this is a mare.” When place and genus are the same, a mark effects otherness: “the cow with black eyes; the cow that is auspicious,” thus. For two <s>āmalaka</s> fruits, because of similarity in genus and mark, difference of place effects otherness: “this one is the former, this one the latter.” But when the former <s>āmalaka</s>, for a knower whose attention is otherwise engaged, is turned to the latter place, then, when the place is the same, the division “this is the former, this is the latter” is untenable. And there must be doubtless true knowledge; therefore it is said, “apprehension is from knowledge born of discrimination”
721: How so? The place co-instantaneous with the former <s>āmalaka</s> is different from the place co-instantaneous with the latter <s>āmalaka</s>, and the two <s>āmalaka</s>-s have distinct experiences of their own place-instants; but the experience of other place-instants is the cause of their otherness. By this example, in the case of a <s>paramāṇu</s> (atom) whose genus, mark, and place are similar, from the direct realization of the co-instantaneousness of the place of the prior atom, if the place of the later atom is not tenable as that place, then the experience of that place by the later atom is different because of the difference of co-instantaneousness; for the Lord, for the <s>yogin</s>, there arises the cognition of otherness of the two
722: Others, however, describe thus—those final particulars (<s>viśeṣa</s>-s) produce the cognition of otherness; there too, difference of place and mark, and difference of genus bounded by corporeal separation (mūrti-vyavadhi), are causes of otherness. But difference of instants is accessible only to the intellect of the <s>yogin</s>; therefore it is said by <s>Vārṣagaṇya</s>: “Because of the absence of difference of corporeal separation, mark, and genus, there is no fundamental distinctness”
723: Knowledge born of discrimination (<s>vivekaja jñāna</s>) is saving (tāraka), pertaining to all objects, in every way pertaining to objects, and non-sequential
725: “Saving” (tārakam) means: arising from one’s own direct awakening, not derived from instruction; “pertaining to all objects” means: for it nothing is left as a non-object; “in every way pertaining to objects” means: it knows past, future, and present, all, in every mode; “non-sequential” means: it grasps all, in every way, mounted upon a single instant. This knowledge born of discrimination is complete; a portion of just this, having taken up the honeyed ground (<s>madhumatī bhūmi</s>) of the lamp of yoga, continues until its completion
726: For one who has attained knowledge born of discrimination, or for one who has not yet attained knowledge born of discrimination—
727: When there is equality of purity of <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>, there is <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation)
729: When the luminosity-nature of the intellect (<s>buddhi-sattva</s>), its rajas and tamas shaken off, becomes one whose sole scope is the cognition of the otherness of <s>Puruṣa</s>, whose seeds of afflictions are burned, then it becomes as though it had assumed the likeness of the purity of <s>Puruṣa</s>; then the absence, by way of figurative attribution, of <s>Puruṣa</s>’s enjoyment is purity. In this state, there is <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation) for the Lord (<s>Īśvara</s>) or the non-Lord alike, whether possessed of knowledge born of discrimination (<s>vivekaja-jñāna</s>) or the other. For knowledge in which the seeds of afflictions have been burned has no further need at all; by the door of the purity of <s>sattva</s> this sovereignty born of <s>samādhi</s> and knowledge has been attained. But in the ultimate truth, non-seeing (ignorance) ceases through knowledge; when that is ceased, there are no subsequent afflictions. From the absence of afflictions, there is the absence of karmic ripening; and in this state, the <s>guṇa</s>-s, having exhausted their mandate, do not again present themselves to <s>Puruṣa</s> as the seen. The <s>kaivalya</s> of that <s>Puruṣa</s> [ensues]; then <s>Puruṣa</s>, pure, a mere light of its own essential form, stainless, becomes solitary (kevalin)
730: Thus ends, in the venerable exposition of <s>Pātañjali</s> on <s>Sāṃkhya</s>, in the Yoga treatise, the third chapter, the Vibhūti-pāda, in the commentary of <s>Vyāsa</s>, 3
732: Perfections (<s>siddhi</s>-s) are born of birth, herbs, mantra, austerity (<s>tapas</s>), or <s>samādhi</s>
734: Siddhi by birth is being endowed with a body other than the human; by herbs, such as the elixir in the mansions of the Asuras; by mantras, attainment of going through <s>ākāśa</s> and of powers beginning with minuteness (<s>aṇimā</s>); by austerity (<s>tapas</s>), the accomplishment of resolves—assuming forms at will, at any place, enjoying as one desires; and the siddhi-s born of <s>samādhi</s> have been explained in this manner
735: There, concerning the body and senses, when they have been transformed into a different species—
736: Transformation into another species is from the filling-up of the nature (<s>prakṛti</s>-s)
738: For them, the cessation of the prior transformation and the arising of the subsequent transformation occurs through the entrance of unprecedented parts; and the natures (<s>prakṛti</s>-s) of the body and senses each support their own modification by a filling-up, while depending on causes such as dharma, and the like
739: The auxiliary cause is not a direct instigator of the natures (<s>prakṛti</s>-s); rather, the removal of the obstruction is from that, like a field-tender
741: For causes such as dharma are not an instigator of the natures (<s>prakṛti</s>-s); a cause is not set into motion by its effect—how then? Rather, the removal of the obstruction is from that, like a field-tender. Just as a field-tender, wishing to flood another plot from a plot already filled with water, does not draw the water out with his hands, whether level or lower, but breaks their obstruction; when that is broken, the waters themselves flood the other plot, so dharma breaks the obstructing property of the natures; when that is broken, the natures themselves inundate their own modifications. Or, as that same field-tender, in that very plot, has no power to make watery or earthy juices enter the seeds of grain, what then does he do? He removes mung, millet, black-grain, and the like; when those are removed, the juices themselves enter the seeds of grain. Likewise, dharma is merely a cause of the cessation of adharma, because of the total opposition of purity and impurity, but dharma is not a cause of the activation of the natures (<s>prakṛti</s>-pravṛtti). Here one should cite <s>Nandīśvara</s> and others; conversely, adharma obstructs dharma, hence the transformation into impurity; and there too one should cite <s>Nahuṣa</s> become a serpent, and the like
742: But when a yogin fashions many bodies, then are they of one mind, or of many minds?—
745: Taking mere <s>asmitā</s> as the cause of mind, he makes constructed minds; therefore they become minded (endowed with minds)
746: In differences of activity, a single mind is the instigator for many
748: How is it that, for many minds, activity proceeds with a single mind’s intention in the forefront?—thus: a single mind fashions the instigator (director) of all the minds, then there is diversity of activities
749: Among those, the one born of meditation (<s>dhyāna</s>) is without deposit (anāśaya)
751: The constructed mind is fivefold; perfections (<s>siddhi</s>-s) are born of birth, herbs, mantra, austerity (<s>tapas</s>), or <s>samādhi</s>. Among these, that very mind which is born of meditation (<s>dhyāna</s>) is indeed without deposit (anāśaya); for that alone there is no deposit—no activation of passion and the rest, no connection with merit and demerit—because the <s>yogin</s> has afflictions worn away; but for the others there is a karmic deposit (karmāśaya)
753: The karma of the <s>yogin</s> is neither white nor black; it is threefold for the others
755: This genus of karma is indeed four-limbed: black, white-and-black, white, and not-white-not-black. There, black is of evil-minded persons; white-and-black is that accomplished by external means. There, by the doorway of harming others and of benefiting (others) alone, there is accumulation of karmic deposit; white belongs to those possessed of austerity (<s>tapas</s>), self-recitation (<s>svādhyāya</s>), and meditation (<s>dhyāna</s>). For that, being dependent on mind alone, not relying on external means, it comes to be without harming others. Not-white-not-black belongs to renouncers whose afflictions are worn away, of the final bodies; therein, not-white is only for the <s>yogin</s> because of the renunciation of the fruit, and not-black is from non-appropriation; but for the other beings, previously, it is threefold
756: Then, there is manifestation only of those dispositions (vāsanā-s) that are in accordance with the ripenings of that (karma)
758: Then—namely, from threefold karma—“only of those that are in accordance with the ripenings of that”: whatever kind of karma’s ripening there is, the dispositions that are in accordance with that, which follow upon karmic ripening, only those are manifested. For indeed a divine karma, when ripening, cannot possibly be the occasion for the manifestation of hellish, animal, or human dispositions; rather, only dispositions in accordance with the divine are manifested for it; and likewise in hellish, animal, and human (cases) the discussion is the same
759: Even for those separated by class (birth), place, and time, there is uninterrupted succession (ānantarya), because memory and latent impression (saṃskāra) have one and the same form
761: The arising of the ripening of a bull’s bite (i.e., the sting of a scorpion), manifested by its own manifesters—if that were separated by a hundred births, or by a far-off place, or by a hundred aeons, yet, when it arises again from that very same its-own-manifester, it would arise swiftly—thus, the disposition fashioned by the prior-experienced ripening of the bull’s bite would, taking up (its cause), be manifested. Why? Because, even for things separated, there exists a cause that is similar, a karma-manifester, having become the occasion; therefore there is indeed uninterrupted succession. And why further? Because memory and latent impression have one and the same form: as the experiences, so the impressions; and these are in conformity with karmic dispositions. And as the dispositions, so the memory; thus, from the impressions separated by class (birth), place, and time, there is memory; and again from memory, impressions—thus, these memory-and-impressions, because they are made to obtain the function of karmic deposit, are manifested; and therefore, because the relation of occasion and occasioned is not cut off even for separated things, uninterrupted succession (ānantarya) is indeed established
762: And their beginninglessness too, because desire (āśiṣ) is eternal
764: Of those dispositions, because desire is eternal, there is beginninglessness. This wish of the self—“May I not be; may I be again”—is seen in everyone; it is not innate (by nature). Why? How would there be, in a living being just born, who has not experienced the property of death, fear of death arising from the memory of suffering linked with aversion? And a thing that is by nature does not take up an occasion. Therefore, this mind, pierced by beginningless dispositions, obtains only certain dispositions according to occasion, and turns back toward the enjoyment of <s>Puruṣa</s>
765: Some, however, have understood: the mind, like a pot, a palace, or a lamp, is contracting and expanding, only of the measure of the body’s size-and-form; and thus, the absence of an inner (self) and <s>saṃsāra</s> (cyclic existence) too would be reasonable
766: The activity (vṛtti) alone of this all-pervading mind (<s>vibhu</s>) called <s>citta</s> is contracting-and-expanding—thus the Teacher; and that depends upon conditions such as dharma and the rest. And the condition is twofold—external and internal. External is that which depends on instruments such as body and the rest—praise, giving, salutation, and the like; internal is faith (<s>śraddhā</s>) and so on, dependent on mind alone. And thus it has been said—“And those diversions (vihāra) of meditators consisting of friendliness (<s>maitrī</s>) and so on, being of the nature of not relying on external instruments, effect dharma in an eminent degree.” Of these two, the mental is stronger. How so? By what would knowledge and dispassion be excelled; and who, apart from superiority of mental power, would undertake by bodily action to make the <s>Daṇḍakāraṇya</s> forest empty, or drink the ocean like <s>Agastya</s>?
767: Because they are bound together by cause, fruit, substratum, and object, with the absence of these, there is the absence of that
769: Cause: from dharma, pleasure; from adharma, pain; from pleasure, attachment (<s>rāga</s>); from pain, aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>); and from those, effort (<s>prayatna</s>)—thus, being set into motion by that, with mind, speech, or body, one greatly favors or harms; from that, again, dharma and adharma, pleasure and pain, attachment and aversion—thus is this six-spoked wheel of <s>saṃsāra</s> set in motion. And of this, as it turns at every instant, ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) is the leader, the root of all afflictions—this is the cause. As for fruit: that, resorting to which, there is the arising-in-presence of dharma and the rest; for there is no production of what is unprecedented. And the mind is the qualified substratum (<s>āśraya</s>) of dispositions (vāsanā-s); for, in a mind whose qualified function is concluded, dispositions, being without substratum, are not able to remain. That object which has become faced-toward (abhimukhī-bhūta), the disposition that manifests it—of that disposition, that is the object (ālambana). Thus, by these four—cause, fruit, substratum, and object—all dispositions are bound together; with the absence of these, there is the absence of the dispositions that rely upon them
770: “There is no coming-to-be of what is not; nor is there destruction of what is”—if dispositions exist as substances, how will they cease?—
771: The past and the future exist in their own nature; because of the division of the path (<s>adhvan</s>) of the properties (<s>dharma</s>-s)
773: The future is particularized as what is-to-become-manifest; the past is particularized as what-has-been-experienced; the present is mounted upon its own operation—this triad is the knowable of knowledge. And if this did not exist in its own nature, this knowledge would not arise as having an object; therefore, the past and the future exist in their own nature. Moreover, if the fruit of karma—whether belonging to enjoyment or belonging to release (<s>apavarga</s>)—that is about to arise were indescribable, then undertaking what is skillful with that as its aim, with that as its condition, would not be reasonable. And a condition with respect to an existent fruit is competent to bring it into presentness, not established for generating the unprecedented; the condition bestows specific favor upon what is conditionally produced, but does not produce the unprecedented
774: And the substratum (<s>dharmin</s>) has the nature of many properties, and its properties are fixed according to the division of the path; and not, as the present, which has attained a particular manifestation, does the past and future exist as a substance in that way. How then? The future exists by its own nature as subtle, by its own suggestive power; and the past, by its own nature as what has been experienced in particular. Thus, manifestation of the form of the path belongs only to the present path; and it does not belong to the past and future paths. And at one and the same time of a single path, two paths, together with the substratum, would arise—that indeed would occur; therefore there is no coming-to-be without having been, of the three paths
775: They are manifest-and-subtle, having the nature of the <s>guṇa</s>-s
777: These very properties, pertaining to the three paths, are present as manifest in the present, and as subtle in the past and future, having the form of the six particularities; in ultimate truth, this all is merely a particular arrangement of the <s>guṇa</s>-s; and thus the scriptural instruction—
779: The supreme form of the <s>guṇa</s>-s does not come within the range of vision,
780: but whatever has come into the range of vision is, like <s>māyā</s> (illusion), exceedingly trifling
782: But if all the <s>guṇa</s>-s are [asked about thus:] how is it that one word is one sense-faculty?—
783: Because of the oneness of transformation, the real nature of the thing (vastu) [is one]
785: Since the <s>guṇa</s>-s, whose nature is manifestation, activity, and stability, are of the nature of being apprehended, as instruments there is a single transformation that is the ear as a sense-faculty; and of the nature of being apprehended (as objects), as the subtle-element of sound (<s>śabda-tanmātra</s>), there is a single transformation that is sound as an object; and for sound and the like, which are of the same genus as formed things (gross forms), there is a single transformation that is the earth-atom (<s>pṛthivī-paramāṇu</s>), [namely] the parts of the subtle-element of earth; and for those, there is a single transformation: “earth, cow, tree, mountain,” and so on—likewise, in the other elements too, taking common properties such as viscosity, heat, plasticity (pliability), and capacity to provide space, the commonality as a single inception of modification ought to be established
786: There is no object accompanied by cognition; but cognition accompanied by an object does exist—[yet] in dream and the like it is fabricated: in this manner, those who deny the very nature of a real thing (vastu), saying, “the thing is only a mere construction by cognition, like a dream-object; it does not exist ultimately,”—how would these who, though this real thing has presented itself by its own greatness, abandon the very nature of the real thing by the strength of a non-pramāṇa-type, conceptual cognition, and refute that very thing—be worthy of credence?
788: Because, when the object is the same, from the difference of minds, the two have divergent paths
790: A single object, which becomes a support for many minds, is common; and indeed it is neither fabricated by one mind nor fabricated by many minds, but rather established in itself. How so? When the object is the same, from the difference of minds: dependent on merit (dharma), even with the object the same, there arises a cognition of pleasure; dependent on demerit (adharma), from that very same [object], a cognition of pain; dependent on ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>), from that very same [object], a deluded cognition; dependent on right vision (samyag-darśana), from that very same [object], a neutral cognition—thus. For whom is that fabricated by whose mind? And it is not reasonable that the coloring (modification) of one’s mind should be effected by an object fabricated by another’s mind. Therefore, for the object and for knowledge—distinct by the difference of the grasped and the grasper—their paths are separate; there is not even a scent of intermixture between these two
791: But, according to the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> position, the object is three-<s>guṇa</s>-ed and unstable—consisting in the activity of the <s>guṇa</s>-s—and, dependent on conditions such as merit and so on, it is connected with minds; and when a cognition arises corresponding to a condition, the condition becomes the cause in that very particular manner. Some say: “the object indeed coexists with cognition, because it is an object of enjoyment, like pleasure and the rest”—and these, by this very doorway, contradicting commonality, deny the very nature of the real thing (vastu) in successive moments,
792: Nor is the object dependent on a single mind—for that would lack pramāṇa; what then would it be?
794: If the object were dependent on a single mind, then, when that mind is engaged, restrained, or manifest in its own form and not touching [the object], the object, being not within the scope of another, would be without pramāṇa, having a nature not apprehended by anyone—what then would that be at that time? And, when it becomes connected again with a mind, whence would it arise? And those parts of it that are not present would not belong to it; thus, if “the back does not exist,” then the belly too would not be apprehended. Therefore, the object is independent, common to all persons; and the minds, being independent, operate individually for each person; from the relation of those two there is apprehension, which is the enjoyment (<s>bhoga</s>) of <s>Puruṣa</s>
795: Because the mind depends upon the coloring (adventitious coloration) by that, an object is known or unknown
797: Objects are like a lodestone-jewel: having connected with the mind, which is of an iron-like nature, they tinge (dye) it; and by whatever object the mind is tinged, that object is known, another, then, is unknown. Since the object has the nature of being known-or-unknown, the mind is that which undergoes transformation
798: But for whom that very mind is the object, for him—
799: The mental activities (<s>citta-vṛtti</s>-s) are always known by the Lord of that (mind), the <s>Puruṣa</s>, because he is unchanging (apariṇāmin)
801: If the Lord, the <s>Puruṣa</s>, were to undergo transformation like the mind (<s>citta</s>), then the mental activities (<s>citta-vṛtti</s>-s) whose object is that (Lord) would be, like objects such as sound, sometimes known and sometimes unknown; but the constant knowability of the mind belongs to it because the Lord of that (mind), the <s>Puruṣa</s>, is unchanging—this is inferred
802: An objection might be raised: the mind itself will be self-luminous and luminous in respect of objects, like fire—
803: It is not self-luminous, because it is seen
805: Just as the other senses and also sound and the rest, because they are objects of sight (i.e., are seen), are not self-luminous, so too the mind should be understood; nor is fire an apt example here, for fire does not illuminate its own nature which is non-manifest, and this illumination is observed in the conjunction of illuminable and illuminator; nor is there conjunction with mere own-nature; moreover, “the mind is self-luminous” would mean “it is ungraspable by anyone”—such is the import of the words. For example, “space is grounded in itself, not grounded in another”—the meaning is this: the activities of the intellect (buddhi) are observed from the reflexive awareness of the movement of one’s own cognition—“I am angry, I am afraid, here I have attachment, there I have anger”—this would not be reasonable if there were no apprehension of one’s own cognition
806: And at one and the same time there is no determination of both
808: Nor is it reasonable that, in a single moment, there be determination of one’s own form and another’s form, given the admission by the momentariness-theorists that what is coming-to-be is itself the action and that very thing is the agent
809: One might think: a mind, blocked by its own savor (i.e., engrossed in its own object), is grasped by another mind that is immediately adjacent—
810: If mind were seen by another mind, there would be an over-proliferation of intellects cognizing intellects, and a confusion of memories
812: If the mind were grasped by another mind, by what would the intellect-cognizing-intellect be grasped? By yet another, and that too by yet another—thus an infinite regress. And there would be a confusion of memories: as many as are the experiences of intellects cognizing intellects, so many memories would ensue; from that intermixing there would be non-determination of a single memory. In this way, by those nihilists who repudiate the <s>Puruṣa</s>, the witness of the intellect, everything is thrown into disorder. They, positing a nature of enjoyer (experiencer) somewhere or other, do not accord with reason; some even fabricate a mere “sentience” (sattva-mātra), saying, “There is that sentient one who, depositing these five aggregates (<s>skandha</s>-s) and assembling other parts, [acts],” and then again they shrink back from that very (position). Likewise, having said, “For the great disenchantment, for dispassion, for the non-arising, for the pacification of the aggregates, I will live the celibate life in the presence of a teacher,” they then deny again the very sentience of the sentient. But the doctrines such as <s>Sāṃkhya</s> and <s>Yoga</s>, in their own terms, arrive at the <s>Puruṣa</s> as the master of the mind (<s>citta</s>) and the enjoyer
814: Because, while consciousness (<s>citi</s>) does not transmigrate, when the mind assumes that form, there is reflexive awareness of one’s own cognition
816: For the power of the enjoyer is unchanging and non-transmigrating, yet, in the presence of a changing object, as it were transmigrating, it follows that very activity; and of that (power), whose nature is reception of appropriated consciousness when it has been obtained, the cognitive activity of the intellect (buddhi-vṛtti), merely as an imitation of it, is designated a cognition-activity not distinct from the intellect-activity. And so it has been said,
818: Neither the netherworld, nor the clefts of mountains, nor darkness, nor the bellies of the oceans,
819: the cave in which the eternal <s>Brahma</s> is hidden—the sages discover as not distinct from the activity of the intellect”
822: The mind (<s>citta</s>), dyed by seer and seen, is all-purpose (capable of all objects)
824: For the mind indeed, being tinged by the object to be thought, and that very [mind], because of being an object, being bound to the subject, the <s>Puruṣa</s>, by the mind’s own mode (vṛtti), therefore this very mind (<s>citta</s>), dyed by seer and seen, appearing as object and subject, having assumed the nature of sentient and insentient, though of the nature of object yet as if not of the nature of object, as if insentient though sentient, like a crystal jewel, is said to be all-purpose (capable of all objects)
825: Accordingly, through this likeness of mind with [both], some, being deluded, say that very [mind] is the sentient principle; others say, “this all is mere mind only; indeed there is not this world of cow and the like, pot and the like, along with causes,”—they are to be pitied. Why? For they have the seed of their error in this: “the mind has the appearance of all-forms.” In <s>samādhi</s>-wisdom, the knowable object, having become a reflection (pratibimba), is other, because it has become the support (ālambana) of that [wisdom]. If the object were mere mind, how would what is of the nature of cognition be determined by cognition alone? Therefore, the object, having become a reflection in the wisdom, by which it is determined—that [determinant] is the <s>Puruṣa</s>. Thus, due to the distinction of the mind by the natures of grasper, grasping, and grasped, all three are divided by kind; those with right vision (<s>samyag-darśin</s>-s), by these [means], apprehend the <s>Puruṣa</s>
827: Because, although variegated by innumerable dispositions (<s>vāsanā</s>-s), it is for-another’s-sake, since it acts as a conjunction-made (a product of assemblage)
829: Thus, this mind, even though variegated precisely by innumerable <s>vāsanā</s>-s, is for-another’s-sake—namely for another’s enjoyment (<s>bhoga</s>) and liberation (<s>apavarga</s>)—not for its own sake, because it acts as a conjunction-made (like a house). A mind that acts as a conjunction-made ought not to be for its own sake: a pleasurable mind is not for the sake of pleasure [itself], nor is knowledge for the sake of knowledge—both of these are for-another’s-sake. And that person who is rich in purpose by enjoyment and by liberation—that indeed is the Other (the beyond), the <s>Puruṣa</s>, not a mere generality. Whatever the nihilists (<s>vaināśika</s>-s) might adduce as some “other” that is a mere generality in its own nature, all that, because it acts as a conjunction-made, would be for-another’s-sake. But that Other which is a particular (viśeṣa) is not a conjunction-made—[that] is the <s>Puruṣa</s>
830: For one who sees the Particular (the discerner), cessation of the imagining of selfhood
832: Just as, in the rainy season, from the sprouting of a grass-shoot the existence of its seed is inferred, so too, for one in whom, upon hearing the path to liberation, horripilation and tears are seen, there too the seed of vision of the Particular (viśeṣa), belonging to liberation, produced by karma—this is inferred. For him, there naturally proceeds the imagining of selfhood (ātma-bhāva-bhāvanā); in the absence of which, the following has been said: setting aside nature, because of defect and the like, there is fondness in the prima facie view and distaste at the conclusion. There, the imagining of selfhood is [such as:] “Who was I? How was I? What is this? How indeed is this? Who shall we be? Or how shall we be?” But that [imagining] ceases for the one who sees the Particular; why? because this manifold transformation belongs to the mind itself, whereas the <s>Puruṣa</s>, in the non-existence of <s>avidyā</s>, is pure, untouched by the properties of the mind. Therefore the imagining of selfhood ceases for the skillful one
833: Then the mind is slanted toward discrimination, weighted toward isolation (<s>kaivalya</s>)
835: Then, that mind of his which was previously weighted toward objects and inclined toward ignorance becomes otherwise—namely, weighted toward <s>kaivalya</s> and inclined by knowledge born of discrimination (<s>viveka</s>)
836: In the gaps of that, other conceptions arise from impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>-s)
838: In the gaps of that mind, which is slanted to discriminative conceptions and flows only with the cognition of the otherness of <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>, other conceptions—“I am,” or “mine,” or “I know,” or “I do not know”—[arise]. Why? From prior impressions, whose seeds are being exhausted
839: The abandonment of these has been stated like the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>-s)
841: Just as the afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>-s), having the condition of seeds burned, are not capable of sprouting, so too the prior impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>-s), having the condition of seeds burned by the fire of knowledge, do not generate further cognitions; whereas the impressions of knowledge, following upon the completion of the mind’s jurisdiction, accompany (only) as an aftermath and therefore are not to be reckoned (as producing new cognitions)
842: For one who is not complacent even in discriminative contemplation (<s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>), there is, in every way, the cognition of discrimination (<s>viveka-khyāti</s>); [then] the cloud-of-dharma (<s>dharma-megha</s>) <s>samādhi</s>
844: When this <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> is not complacent even in <s>prasaṃkhyāna</s>, then he desires nothing even beyond that; for one who is dispassionate even therein, there arises in every way only <s>viveka-khyāti</s>, and because of the exhaustion of the seeds of impressions, no other cognitions arise for him; then for him there is the <s>samādhi</s> named “cloud-of-dharma” (<s>dharma-megha</s>)
845: Thereupon, cessation of afflictions and karma (<s>kleśa</s>- and <s>karma</s>-cessation)
847: By the attainment of that, the afflictions beginning with <s>avidyā</s> are cut up by the root, and the stores of karma (<s>karmāśaya</s>-s), both wholesome and unwholesome, are struck down by the root; upon the cessation of afflictions and karma, the knower, even while living, becomes liberated—why? because misapprehension (<s>viparyaya</s>) is the cause of becoming (saṃsāra); for no one anywhere is ever seen to be born with misapprehension extinct
848: Then, because of the infinity of knowledge, from which all coverings and stains are removed, the knowable is small
850: For knowledge, freed from all coverings of afflictions and karma, there is infinitude; the existent of knowledge (<s>jñāna-sattva</s>), infinite, overpowered and covered by the covering darkness, being at some time set in motion by <s>rajas</s>, opened up, becomes capable of apprehension; there, when it becomes freed from all covering-stains, then it attains infinitude; and because of the infinitude of knowledge, the knowable becomes little—like a firefly in the sky; as this has been said—
852: The blind man did not pierce the jewel, the fingerless one set it in motion toward him,
853: the neckless one wore it, the tongueless one offered it worship,”
855: Then, for those whose purpose is accomplished, there is the completion of the sequence of transformations of the <s>guṇa</s>-s
857: From the rise of that cloud-of-dharma, the sequence of transformations of the <s>guṇa</s>-s—whose purpose is accomplished—is brought to completion; for those whose enjoyment and liberation (<s>bhoga</s> and <s>apavarga</s>) have been accomplished, whose sequence is brought to an end, do not endure even for a moment
858: Now, what is this sequence, called “sequence”—
859: Sequence is that which is apprehended at the other end (termination) of a transformation, with a moment as its counterpart
861: Sequence, whose nature is the unbroken succession of moments, is grasped by the conclusion (other-end) of a transformation; for there is no oldness at the end of a cloth for moments of sequence not experienced, and in what is eternal sequence is observed
862: And this eternality is twofold: rock-steady eternality and transforming eternality; there, rock-steady eternality belongs to the <s>Puruṣa</s>, transforming eternality to the <s>guṇa</s>-s; that in which, while transforming, the reality is not subverted—that is eternal; and, because the realities of both are not struck down, there is eternality; there, in the properties of the <s>guṇa</s>-s—such as intellect (<s>buddhi</s>) and the rest—the sequence, apprehended at the termination of a transformation, has obtained its conclusion, but in the eternal substrates, the <s>guṇa</s>-s, it has not obtained a conclusion; in those who are rock-steadily eternal, established only in their own nature—the liberated <s>Puruṣa</s>-s—the existence of their own nature is experienced indeed only in sequence, therefore there too it has not obtained a conclusion; this (view), taking up the affirmation “there is” from the back of the word (i.e., from verbal usage), is a construction (a conceptual posit)
863: Now, as to this saṃsāra—does there exist a completion of sequence in the <s>guṇa</s>-s in which it abides by its persistence and movement, or not? This is inexpressible; how could it be?—the question “Is it?” is absolutely answerable: “All who are born will die”—om, sir
864: Now, “All who have died will be born”—this ought to be stated by distinguishing cases. The one in whom discriminative cognition (<s>khāti</s> [scil. <s>pratyudita-khyāti</s>]) has arisen and craving is exhausted, the skillful one, will not be born; but the other will be born. Likewise, regarding the human kind: “Is it better (more conducive to <s>śreyas</s>) or not better?”—when asked thus, the question ought to be answered by distinguishing cases: in regard to beasts it is not better, in regard to the gods and <s>ṛṣi</s>-s it is better. But this question is unstateable: “Is this <s>saṃsāra</s> finite or infinite?” Determining on either side—“for the skillful one there is completion of the sequence of <s>saṃsāra</s>, not for the other”—there is a defect; therefore, indeed this question ought to be declined (not taken up)
865: At the completion of the sequence governing the jurisdiction of the <s>guṇa</s>-s, <s>kaivalya</s> was stated; its own nature is to be ascertained—
866: The involution (<s>pratiprasava</s>) of the <s>guṇa</s>-s that are devoid of purpose for the <s>Puruṣa</s> is <s>kaivalya</s>, or the establishment in one’s own form; that is, the power of consciousness (<s>citi-śakti</s>)
868: For those <s>guṇa</s>-s whose enjoyment and liberation (<s>bhoga</s> and <s>apavarga</s>) have been accomplished and which are devoid of purpose for the <s>Puruṣa</s>, that involution of the <s>guṇa</s>-s whose nature is effect-and-cause—that is <s>kaivalya</s>; but establishment in one’s own form, due to the non-connection of the <s>Puruṣa</s> with the <s>buddhi</s>-<s>sattva</s>, is the power of consciousness (<s>citi-śakti</s>) alone, isolated; the perpetual abiding of that just so is <s>kaivalya</s>
869: Thus ends, in the Yoga treatise, the exposition of <s>Sāṃkhya</s> by the venerable <s>Patañjali</s>, in <s>Vyāsa</s>’s commentary, the fourth chapter, the Kaivalya Section—4
